claim: Human: biallelic loss-of-function mutations in CCN6 (WISP3) cause progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia, a postnatal disorder with onset at about 3 to 8 years and continued cartilage loss, so the gene is needed for cartilage maintenance after birth. The mouse knockout reportedly has no skeletal phenotype (seen only as a search-result title, not opened).
verify_reason: PubMed abstract of PMID 10471507 (Hurvitz et al., Nat Genet 1999) read: nine different WISP3 mutations in unrelated patients with autosomal recessive progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia; symptoms start at 3 to 8 years, with continued cartilage loss and joint replacement by the third decade; no extraskeletal manifestations; authors conclude the gene is essential for normal postnatal skeletal growth and cartilage homeostasis. Positional cloning is gene-specific. The evidence is human genetics in a childhood-onset disease that progresses into adulthood, not an expression measurement in normal adult tissue. UniProt O95389 also cites this paper for expression in synoviocytes and articular chondrocytes. The mouse-knockout part of the claim was not checked (I did not locate that paper).
criteria_gap: Cartilage is not in the HPA/GTEx bulk panels or the rare-cell screen organs; CCN6 has no literature verdict, and its top listed off-target tissue is cerebellum at 3.5 TPM.

claim: Human: immunohistochemistry shows WISP3 protein in midzone chondrocytes of normal adult articular cartilage, and WISP3 raises type II collagen and aggrecan expression in chondrocyte lines.
verify_reason: PubMed abstract of PMID 14872491 (Sen et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004) read: immunohistochemistry with an anti-WISP3 antibody shows WISP3 protein in midzone chondrocytes of normal adult human articular cartilage (also in osteoarthritic clusters and fetal growth cartilage); WISP3 transfection raises type II collagen and aggrecan in human chondrocyte lines C-28/I2 and T/C-28a2, and a PPRD mutant is impaired. Caveat: only the abstract was read, so antibody validation against other CCN family members was not checked; it is a single 2004 IHC study.
criteria_gap: Protein evidence in a tissue absent from HPA IHC and from every RNA panel the screen uses.

claim: Human: UniProt curates LRRC52 tissue specificity as 'mainly expressed in testis and skeletal muscle', citing Yan and Aldrich 2012 (PMID 22547800). The abstract of that paper, which I read, names only testis, so the skeletal muscle statement rests on the UniProt annotation of the paper's tissue panel.
best_source: PMID 22547800, full text PMC3356614, Fig. 4 and Discussion
verify_reason: The finding said the muscle statement rested only on UniProt. The full text of Yan and Aldrich 2012 (PMC3356614) states it directly: 'LRRC52 is dominantly expressed in testis and skeletal muscle. A much lower level of LRRC52 expression was also detected in several other tissues including placenta, kidney, lung, and some glands' (Fig. 4, TaqMan real-time PCR on a normal human tissue panel, relative to RPLP0). The paralogs LRRC26, LRRC38 and LRRC55 were assayed separately with distinct patterns, so the assay is gene-specific. Caveats: relative mRNA only, plotted on a log scale, no protein, presumably a commercial adult RNA panel, and LRRC38 is also muscle-expressed in the same figure.
criteria_gap: Skeletal muscle is in the bulk panels, yet the catalog's highest off-target is parathyroid at 3.8 TPM. A gene-specific assay reporting muscle expression is not captured by an atlas maximum; worth checking the muscle value directly.

claim: Human: UniProt (Q96PH6) states DEFB118 is epididymis-specific at high level but 'also expressed in pancreas', attributing this to PMID 12600824. The abstract of that paper does not mention pancreas, so I could not confirm it in the primary source.
verify_reason: UniProt Q96PH6 TISSUE SPECIFICITY reads 'High-level and epididymis-specific expression... Also expressed in pancreas (PubMed:12600824)'. The claim is accurate as stated, including its own caveat: the abstract of PMID 12600824 does not mention pancreas and I could not open the full text, so the primary data (level, assay detail) remain unverified. Treat as curated-annotation evidence only.
criteria_gap: The catalog shows 0.0 TPM off-target, so a cDNA-panel PCR contradicts the atlases for pancreas. It may reflect a minor cell population or a low-level PCR signal.

claim: The human cloning paper reports GALR3 mRNA highly expressed in human testis and detectable in adrenal gland and pancreas. Rat data (same era, PMID 9722565 abstract seen in search results only) describe a widely distributed, low-abundance transcript highest in hypothalamus and pituitary.
verify_reason: Abstract of PMID 9832121 read: 'GALR3 mRNA was highly expressed in human testis and was detectable in adrenal gland and pancreas.' The rat statement also matches PMID 9722565 (widely distributed, low abundance, highest in hypothalamus and pituitary by RNase protection). Caveats: 'detectable' only, a 1998 assay whose method and tissue source (probably commercial adult RNA) are not given in the abstract, with no cell-type localisation and no protein. It supports a low-level signal, not a functional role.
criteria_gap: Low-abundance GPCR transcripts sit below the bulk TPM cut-off (catalog max 2.2 TPM in hypothalamus); gene-specific assays detect it in adrenal and pancreas, which the atlas values do not flag.

claim: Human: OMIM and UniProt summaries of Lindahl et al. 2001 state GFRA4 transcripts are highly expressed in adult human thyroid, with RT-PCR and in situ hybridisation localising it to C cells (normal and medullary carcinoma). The primary paper was not opened in this session.
source: https://omim.org/entry/618679 (seen in search results; fetch returned 403)
verify_reason: The primary paper was found and its abstract read (Lindahl et al. 2001, PMID 11116144). The title and abstract state that human GFRA4 splice forms are 'predominantly expressed in the thyroid gland' and that RET and GFRA4, but not other GFRA mRNAs, overlap in 'normal and malignant thyroid medullary cells'. That is human, includes normal tissue, and distinguishes GFRA4 from GFRA1-3. The 'adult thyroid' and 'RT-PCR and in situ' details come from the OMIM summary seen in search results; the abstract does not give the methods or donor age. No human protein-level evidence in normal C cells was seen.
criteria_gap: C cells are well under 1% of thyroid cells, so bulk thyroid RNA shows only 1.3 TPM, and thyroid is not among the organs covered by the donor-level rare-cell screen.

claim: Human: the maternally expressed transcription factor KLF14 is a master trans-regulator of adipose gene expression; its cis-eQTL is associated with type 2 diabetes and HDL cholesterol (Small 2011, MuTHER; replicated in METSIM, PMID 28257690). Reviews found in search report adipocyte-specific Klf14 deletion in mice shifts fat distribution in females, while whole-body knockout in male mice shows no metabolic phenotype.
verify_reason: PMID 21572415 abstract says the T2D- and HDL-associated cis-eQTL of maternally expressed KLF14 acts as a master trans regulator of adipose gene expression (adult human adipose biopsies). PMID 28257690 abstract confirms METSIM replicated and extended the KLF14 trans network to 55 genes. A stronger source is PMID 29632379 (Small 2018): risk alleles reduce KLF14 expression in adipose, KLF14 knockdown in human pre-adipocytes alters proliferation and lipogenesis, and adipose-specific Klf14 deletion in mice partly reproduces insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, with female-specific effects. KLF14 has no close paralog confounding an eQTL at its own locus. The statement that whole-body knockout males show no phenotype was not checked.
criteria_gap: A transcription factor that is functional at very low RNA: adipose expression is below the TPM threshold (catalog maximum is 1.66 TPM, in adrenal), so abundance-based screens pass it even though it has a documented physiological role in a non-reproductive tissue. Monoallelic imprinted expression halves the signal further.

claim: Human: alpha-lactalbumin is the regulatory subunit of lactose synthase, and its normal expression is confined to the breast during late pregnancy and lactation (UniProt P00709; Tuohy 2016). This is hormone-induced expression in a tissue present in every adult woman, and it is the stated limitation of the alpha-lactalbumin breast cancer vaccine programme.
verify_reason: The Tuohy 2016 abstract (PMID 27322324) states alpha-lactalbumin 'expression in normal tissues is confined exclusively to the breast during late pregnancy and lactation', and UniProt P00709 annotates it as 'Mammary gland specific. Secreted in milk.' LALBA is a single well-characterised gene with no paralog ambiguity (its role as the lactose synthase regulatory subunit is textbook). The claim as stated is accurate. Whether it counts as a screen miss depends on whether breast is classed as reproductive in the catalog; it is induced, pregnancy- and lactation-restricted expression in normal adult breast.
criteria_gap: The catalog appears to count this under reproductive tissue (reproductive best 542,438), which hides that the target is massively expressed in lactating breast. If breast is treated as reproductive, the screen cannot distinguish a germ-cell antigen from a lactation protein; this may be expected by design.

tissue: hair follicle (beard, axillary, pubic hair; some scalp vellus hairs)
claim: Human: the type I hair keratin hHa7 (KRT37) is constitutively expressed in medullary cells of all male and female sexual hairs (beard, axillary, pubic) and is a direct androgen-receptor target gene; in scalp it was only detected in some vellus hairs. A 2013 follow-up (PMID 23413938, title only seen) reports androgen-regulated K37 in occipital hair medulla.
verify_reason: PMID 15086535 abstract opened and says exactly this: hHa7 (KRT37) is constitutively expressed in medullary cells of all male and female sexual hairs, was only seen in some scalp vellus hairs, and binds androgen receptor at three promoter AREs (EMSA plus reporter assays). Human, adult, normal skin appendage; body hair is not a reproductive organ. The work is hHa7-specific from the group that defined the individual hair keratins. PMID 23413938 exists with the stated title but has no abstract, so the occipital-medulla detail rests on the title only.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle is not a separate tissue in the bulk panels or the rare-cell screen; skin bulk (5.9 TPM) dilutes it, and expression is androgen-induced and body-site specific (sexual hair), so scalp or trunk skin samples under-represent it.

cell_type: upper cortex and cuticle trichocytes (late differentiation)
claim: Human: K39 is a bona fide type I hair keratin, among the last expressed during hair differentiation (Langbein 2007, completion of the human hair keratin catalog; abstract not available, title only). A 2014 review places K39 in the mid/upper cortex and cuticle, and HPA single-cell data annotate it as enriched in hair cortex cells.
best_source: PMID 17301834 (via UniProt Q6A163 tissue-specificity annotation; also PMID 15617563)
verify_reason: PMID 17301834 exists with the stated title (K39 and K40 are the last keratins expressed in hair differentiation); PubMed has no abstract. UniProt Q6A163, citing that paper and PMID 15617563, states KRT39 is in the upper hair cuticle and upper cortex and in upper beard hairs at protein level. Human, adult, normal, K39-specific. I did not open the J-STAGE review or HPA single-cell page; they are not needed for the claim.
criteria_gap: Structural hair-shaft protein; hair follicle is absent from bulk panels and the rare-cell screen, so only the diluted skin value (5.2 TPM) is seen. The 'Cancer Antigen only' category does not reflect a normal constitutive hair role.

claim: Human: same study as KRTAP10-8; nearly all KAP10 members are expressed exclusively in a narrow band of the hair fiber cuticle in anagen follicles by gene-specific in situ hybridization. Member-level identity is not given in the abstract.
verify_reason: Same evidence as KRTAP10-8: PMID 14962103 abstract supports the cuticle in situ result with gene-specific probes, and PMID 15028290 shows RT-PCR transcripts for all 16 genes of the cluster in hair root only, not in 28 other tissues including skin. UniProt P60371 carries the cuticle annotation for this gene citing both. Caveat: 'nearly all' in the in situ paper means one or more members were not seen by in situ, and the abstract does not say which; the RT-PCR covers all members.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle absent from bulk and rare-cell panels; skin bulk 2.5 TPM is diluted follicle signal. Also flagged mapping_risk because the family is highly similar and intronless.

claim: Human: in situ hybridization on anagen scalp follicles with gene-specific 3' non-coding probes showed nearly all KAP10 and KAP12 family members expressed exclusively in a narrow region of the middle hair fiber cuticle; eight KAP10 cDNAs were isolated from scalp mRNA. The abstract does not name which members, so the assignment to KRTAP10-8 specifically is family-level.
verify_reason: PMID 14962103 abstract says what is claimed (gene-specific 3' non-coding probes; nearly all KAP10/KAP12 members in a narrow band of the mid hair fiber cuticle). The member-level gap the finder noted is closed by PMID 15028290 (Shibuya 2004): RT-PCR detected transcripts for all 16 genes of this 21q22.3 cluster (KRTAP12.1-12.4 and KRTAP18.1-18.12, the old names for the KAP10 genes), restricted to hair root cells and absent from 28 other tissues including skin. UniProt P60410 gives the cuticle annotation for this gene citing both papers. I did not verify the old-to-new name mapping per gene beyond UniProt.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle cuticle is not sampled by bulk panels or the rare-cell screen; skin bulk (7.3 TPM) is the only trace. Normal constitutive expression in a regenerating, non-disposable skin appendage.

claim: Human: the KAP12 family (four members at 21q22.3) is expressed, like KAP10, exclusively in a narrow region of the middle hair fiber cuticle of anagen follicles by in situ hybridization; two KAP12 cDNAs were recovered from scalp mRNA. Whether KRTAP12-4 is one of the detected members is not stated in the abstract.
verify_reason: PMID 14962103 abstract supports the family-level cuticle in situ result, though only two of four KAP12 cDNAs were recovered from scalp. PMID 15028290 names KRTAP12.1-12.4 explicitly and reports RT-PCR transcripts for all of them, restricted to hair root and absent from 28 other tissues including skin. UniProt P60329 annotates this gene as cuticle-restricted. The 'not in 28 other tissues' result also supports the finder's view that the 0.71 TPM blood value is mapping noise.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle not in panels. The catalog's top off-target tissue is blood (0.71 TPM), which is probably mapping noise; the real normal site (hair cuticle) is unsampled.

claim: Human: RT-PCR across a variety of organs detected KAP24.1 only in scalp, and in situ hybridization plus immunofluorescence with a KAP24.1 antibody showed specific expression in the middle/upper hair cuticle (Rogers 2007).
verify_reason: PubMed abstract of PMID 17235325 (Rogers 2007, J Invest Dermatol) says exactly this: RT-PCR of a variety of organs found KAP24.1 only in human scalp, and in situ hybridization plus immunofluorescence with a KAP24.1-derived antibody showed specific expression in the middle/upper hair cuticle. UniProt Q3LI83 carries the same annotation citing this paper. KAP24.1 has no close family members (the paper notes no association with other KAPs), so the assay is gene-specific. Hair-follicle structural protein only; no vital-tissue finding.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle is not a separate tissue in the bulk panels or the rare-cell screen; bulk skin (6.0 TPM here) dilutes a follicle-restricted structural protein, so the low value understates constitutive protein expression in normal adult hair.

claim: Human: Human Protein Atlas places KRTAP29-1 in a skin RNA expression cluster annotated 'Hair follicle development'; no gene-specific expression study was found and UniProt A8MX34 lists no tissue specificity.
verify_reason: Checked the HPA record for ENSG00000212658: tissue expression cluster is 'Cluster 9: Skin - Hair follicle development', RNA tissue specificity 'Tissue enriched' with skin 1.7 nTPM, detected in a single tissue, not detected in immune cells, brain or single-cell data; HPA evidence is transcript level only. UniProt A8MX34 has no tissue specificity. Claim is accurate as stated but is atlas-only: it is the same data the screen already uses, at very low level, with no independent assay.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle is not sampled as a tissue; this is the same atlas source the screen already uses, so it adds only the cluster annotation. The catalog's top off-target tissue is blood.

claim: Human: RT-PCR showed expression restricted to hair root and not detected in other tissues (Yahagi 2004; UniProt Q6L8H2 tissue specificity).
verify_reason: UniProt Q6L8H2 curated tissue specificity (ECO:0000269, PMID 15144888): 'Restricted to hair root, not detected in any other tissues'. The Yahagi 2004 abstract itself only says 'preferential expression in human hair root' for the KRTAP5 genes; the per-gene statement comes from UniProt's curation of the full text, which I could not open. Caveats: plain RT-PCR in a near-identical single-exon family (no sequencing or in situ mentioned in the abstract), so paralog cross-amplification cannot be excluded; gene-specificity is assumed from per-gene results, not verified.
criteria_gap: Hair root/follicle is absent from bulk panels and from the rare-cell screen tissues; skin bulk RNA (7.6 TPM) is only a diluted proxy.

claim: Human: RT-PCR showed expression restricted to hair root and not detected in other tissues (Yahagi 2004; UniProt Q6L8H1).
verify_reason: UniProt Q6L8H1 curated annotation citing PMID 15144888: 'Restricted to hair root, not detected in any other tissues'. Abstract supports hair-root-preferential RT-PCR expression at family level; per-gene detail is from UniProt curation of the full text (not opened). Same caveat as the other KRTAP5 genes: RT-PCR only, near-identical paralogs, primer specificity not verified.
criteria_gap: Hair root/follicle is absent from bulk panels and the rare-cell screen; skin bulk RNA is a diluted proxy.

claim: Human: RT-PCR showed expression restricted to hair root and not detected in other tissues (Yahagi 2004; UniProt Q701N2).
verify_reason: UniProt Q701N2 curated annotation citing PMID 15144888: 'Restricted to hair root, not detected in any other tissues'. Abstract supports hair-root-preferential RT-PCR expression; per-gene detail is from UniProt curation (full text not opened). RT-PCR only in a near-identical family; primer specificity not verified.
criteria_gap: Hair root/follicle is absent from bulk panels and the rare-cell screen; skin bulk RNA is a diluted proxy.

claim: Human: RT-PCR showed expression in hair root but not in skin (Yahagi 2004; UniProt Q6L8G8).
verify_reason: UniProt Q6L8G8 curated annotation citing PMID 15144888: 'Expressed in hair root but not in skin'. Matches the claim. Per-gene detail is from UniProt curation of the full text (not opened); RT-PCR only, primer specificity among KRTAP5 paralogs not verified.
criteria_gap: Hair root/follicle is absent from bulk panels and the rare-cell screen; the paper reports hair root positive where whole skin was negative, so skin bulk RNA is not a reliable proxy.

claim: Human: RT-PCR showed expression restricted to hair root; UniProt P26371 additionally annotates expression in the cuticle layers of differentiating hair follicles at a late stage of fiber differentiation. The catalog's top off-target tissue is blood, which this literature does not support.
verify_reason: UniProt P26371 annotation matches the claim word for word: 'Restricted to hair root, not detected in any other tissues. Expressed in cuticle layers of differentiating hair follicles' (PMID 15144888), developmental stage 'at a late stage of fiber differentiation'. KRTAP5-9 is the long-known KerA/KRN1 gene named in the Yahagi abstract. The cuticle localisation likely derives from the older KerA literature rather than from Yahagi's RT-PCR. No support for blood expression.
criteria_gap: Hair root/follicle cuticle is absent from bulk panels and the rare-cell screen.

tissue: stomach (gastric antrum); also neutrophils, thyroid, lung, kidney
claim: Human: UniProt (Q8WTQ1), citing the original hBD-4 paper (PMID 11481241, 'a novel inducible peptide'), records high expression in testis, relatively high levels in gastric antrum, and lower expression in neutrophils, thyroid, lung and kidney. I read the UniProt annotation only; the paper has no PubMed abstract.
best_source: UniProt Q8WTQ1 (https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8WTQ1.txt), citing Garcia et al. 2001 FASEB J 15:1819, PMID 11481241
verify_reason: UniProt Q8WTQ1 TISSUE SPECIFICITY reads: 'High expression in the testis. Gastric antrum exhibited relatively high levels. A lower expression is observed in uterus and neutrophils thyroid gland, lung, and kidney. No detectable expression in other tissues tested', attributed to PMID 11481241. The claim matches (it omits uterus, which is reproductive anyway). Caveat: the primary paper (Garcia et al. 2001, FASEB J) has no PubMed abstract and I could not open its full text, so the assay details, donor age and quantitation are unverified; confirmation is at the curated-annotation level only. DEFB104A and DEFB104B encode the same protein, so the copy ambiguity does not matter.
criteria_gap: The catalog's highest off-target value is 1.9 TPM in esophagus. Gastric antrum is a subregion that bulk stomach samples may dilute, and neutrophil expression is easily lost in sorted-cell RNA. Any bacterial induction is invisible to steady-state atlases.

claim: Human: Terkawi et al. 2017 (Sci Rep) found DEFB130 among the top three genes upregulated in macrophages phagocytosing Plasmodium falciparum-infected red cells; expression was higher in differentiated macrophages than in monocytes, knockdown increased parasite biomass, and synthetic DEFB130 peptide had modest anti-plasmodial activity.
best_source: Terkawi et al. 2017, Sci Rep 7:41772, PMID 28181499, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5299406
verify_reason: I opened the paper (Terkawi et al. 2017, PMC5299406) and it supports the claim as stated. DEFB130 was one of the top three upregulated genes (about 4.6-fold by microarray, validated by qRT-PCR) in human donor macrophages phagocytosing P. falciparum-infected red cells. ELISA and confocal immunofluorescence showed protein, and levels were higher in differentiated macrophages than in monocytes or THP-1. esiRNA knockdown raised parasite biomass, and the synthetic peptide had modest activity (IC50 about 43-49 uM). Caveats: the macrophages were differentiated in vitro with GM-CSF and IFN-gamma, not taken from tissue; it is a single unreplicated study; absolute expression is not given; the antibody is not knockout-validated. The paper does not distinguish DEFB130A from DEFB130B (it cites NM_001037804), which does not matter for a combined A/B entry.
criteria_gap: Induced rather than constitutive expression: the sorted-immune-cell and bulk blood data are resting state (the CSV's 2.6 TPM blood value is the baseline trace of this), and activated or phagocytosing macrophages are not sampled by any part of the screen.

claim: In human macrophages NLRP11 binds ASC and NLRP3 and is required for NLRP3 inflammasome assembly; NLRP11 deletion blocks NLRP3 activation and siRNA knockdown in primary human macrophages reduces IL-1beta release (Nat Immunol 2022). The gene is absent in mice.
verify_reason: Abstract and PMC full text opened. Gangopadhyay et al., Nat Immunol 2022: NLRP11 is 'an essential component of the NLRP3 inflammasome in human macrophages', interacts with NLRP3 and ASC, and its deletion prevents NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, pyroptosis and cytokine release; re-expression rescues. The full text states IL-1beta release (not IL-6) was reduced in primary human macrophages with siRNA-silenced NLRP11. The abstract states NLRP11 is not expressed in mice. Assays are gene-specific (siRNA, CRISPR knockout, rescue). Caveat: the primary cells are in vitro cultured, LPS-primed macrophages, so this is functional evidence in an induced state, not an in situ tissue expression measurement.
criteria_gap: Bulk blood RNA is only 0.6 TPM and the sorted immune cell panel covers resting cells; differentiated or activated macrophages are not sampled, and the rare-cell screen does not cover immune or bone-marrow compartments. There is no mouse ortholog, so no knockout phenotype would flag it. Only the search-result summary of the abstract was read; the PubMed page did not load.

claim: Human: UniProt P22612 curates germline PRKACG variants (Ile74Met) as the cause of Bleeding disorder, platelet-type, 19 (MIM 616176), a macrothrombocytopenia with platelet dysfunction, citing Manchev et al., Blood 2014. This implies a functional role in the megakaryocyte/platelet lineage, although UniProt's tissue-specificity note still reads 'Testis specific'.
best_source: Manchev VT et al., Blood 2014;124(16):2554-63, PMID 25061177, PMCID PMC4199957 (abstract read); UniProt P22612; OMIM 616176
verify_reason: UniProt P22612 does carry the BDPLT19 (MIM 616176) disease annotation citing PMID 25061177, alongside the 'Testis specific' tissue note. I read the PubMed abstract of Manchev et al., Blood 2014: a consanguineous family with severe autosomal recessive macrothrombocytopenia and thrombocytopathy, homozygous c.222C>G (p.Ile74Met) in PRKACG, with a marked proplatelet-formation defect and low filamin A in megakaryocytes, rescued in vitro by lentiviral wild-type PRKACG in patient megakaryocytes. The rescue makes this gene-specific rather than attributable to PRKACA/PRKACB. Caveats: it is a single family with one missense variant; the evidence is functional in patient megakaryocytes, not a direct measurement of expression in normal tissue; the full text did not load, so the paper's megakaryocyte/platelet expression data remain unchecked.
criteria_gap: Bulk RNA is low (0.42 TPM, top tissue blood) and megakaryocytes/platelets are not in the sorted immune-cell panel or the rare-cell screen (no bone marrow). The gene has no literature verdict. I read only the UniProt entry; the PubMed abstract page would not load, so zygosity and the megakaryocyte expression data in the primary paper are unchecked.

tissue: lymph node and other lymphoid tissue
claim: Human: SCGB1D4 (IIS) is reported as expressed in nearly all tissues, strongest in lymph node, tonsil, cultured lymphoblasts and ovary, and is inducible by interferon-gamma in lymphoblast cells (UniProt, citing PMID 15034037; Jackson et al. 2011 review).
source: PMID 22155607 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3251818) and UniProt SCGB1D4 entry citing PMID 15034037; the primary paper was not opened
best_source: PMID 15034037 (DOI 10.4049/jimmunol.172.7.4245), abstract; corroborated by PMID 21385388 / PMC3063214
verify_reason: Primary abstract (Choi et al., J Immunol 2004, PMID 15034037) says IIS is expressed in virtually all tissues, highest in lymph nodes, tonsil, cultured lymphoblasts and ovary, is augmented by IFN-gamma in lymphoblast cells, and is markedly elevated in activated CD8+ and CD19+ cells versus resting lymphoid cells. UniProt Q6XE38 and the review (PMC3251818) repeat this. Independent support for cytokine induction: Lu et al. 2011 (PMC3063214) found IL-1beta, TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma increased SCGB1D4 in normal human nasal explants using sequenced qRT-PCR products. Caveats: only the abstract of the 2004 paper was read, so I could not check whether its probes exclude the close paralogs SCGB1D1/SCGB1D2; and HPA disagrees on the resting pattern (enriched in fallopian tube, cervix and epididymis, not lymphoid tissue), so the 'all tissues' breadth is doubtful while the induction claim stands.
criteria_gap: Interferon-gamma-induced expression in activated lymphoid cells is not captured by resting bulk tissue or sorted resting immune cell RNA (catalog shows 0.6 TPM in thymus); tonsil is treated as disposable but lymph node is not.

claim: ZNRF4 is an ER-anchored E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades RIP2 and negatively regulates NOD2 signalling: Znrf4-knockdown monocytes showed sustained NF-kB activation, and Znrf4-knockdown mice had reduced NOD2-induced tolerance to MDP and cleared Listeria monocytogenes better. The abstract does not state the species of the monocytes, and the in vivo data are mouse knockdown, not a human expression measurement.
verify_reason: The source exists and supports the claim; the full text (PMC5493756) is stronger than the abstract-only reading. The monocytes are human: THP-1 cells and primary CD14+ monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages from human PBMC. Knockdown of endogenous ZNRF4 in human primary monocytes raised RIP2 protein and NF-kB activation; endogenous ZNRF4 co-immunoprecipitated with RIP2 in primary human monocytes, at a low level unstimulated and more after MDP; ZNRF4 silencing increased IL-8, TNF and IL-1beta secretion in primary human macrophages. Expression is induced: the paper reports ZNRF4 upregulation by NOD2/MDP stimulation and Listeria infection, and enhanced ZNRF4 in peritoneal macrophages of MDP-tolerised mice. The in vivo data are mouse morpholino knockdown, as the claim says. Caveats: endogenous protein detection relies on commercial antibodies (Abcam ab173954/ab67951, Santa Cruz sc-169900) whose specificity is supported by siRNA knockdown shown in cell lines; this is a single laboratory's report with no independent replication found, and it conflicts with near-zero ZNRF4 RNA in sorted immune-cell atlases. ZNRF4 has no close paralog likely to confound the siRNA or qPCR.
criteria_gap: The screen sees 0.4 TPM maximum off-target and nothing in sorted immune cells, yet a functional role is reported in monocytes, with tolerance to MDP implying a stimulus-dependent role. Constitutive bulk and sorted-cell RNA would not capture low-abundance or induced expression in activated myeloid cells. Only the abstract was read, so whether endogenous ZNRF4 protein was shown in primary human monocytes is unverified.

claim: Human: PCR on tissue cDNA panels showed DEFB106 expressed in lung, with in situ hybridization showing tissue- and cell-specific expression (Kao et al. 2003). UniProt summarises it as 'expressed specifically in epididymis and lung'.
best_source: PMID 12600824 (Kao et al. 2003, Am J Respir Cell Mol Biol 29:71); UniProt Q8N104
verify_reason: The abstract of PMID 12600824 says PCR on human tissue cDNA panels confirmed expression and 'Two of them, DEFB106 and DEFB109, were expressed in the lung', and that in situ hybridization with cRNA probes showed 'tissue-/cell-specific expression' of DEFB106. UniProt Q8N104 says 'Expressed specifically in epididymis and lung'. Caveats: the abstract does not name the lung cell type (airway epithelium is implied by the title only), I could not open the full text, and commercial cDNA panels are assumed to be adult normal tissue. DEFB106A/B are identical copies.
criteria_gap: The catalog shows about 0.1 TPM off-target (midbrain) and nothing in lung. A gene-specific PCR and in situ assay contradicts the atlases, possibly because the 8p23 duplicated copies map poorly or because expression sits in a minor airway cell population.

tissue: several nongametogenic adult tissues (not named in abstract)
claim: Human: SPANX-N family reported as expressed at a low level in several nongametogenic adult tissues, in contrast to SPANX-A/D. Family-level statement from the abstract; member-specific tissues not verified.
verify_reason: Full text of PMID 17406683 read; it supports the claim and is more specific than the abstract. Table 2 assigns SPANX-N3 transcripts, by cloning and sequencing of RT-PCR products, to normal adult lung and distal colon as well as prostate and testis; brain, liver, muscle, spleen, heart, kidney and lymph node were negative. Signal was about 50 to 100 times lower than testis. Caveats: qualitative 35-cycle RT-PCR on commercial RNA (Clontech/Ambion, some from normal/tumor pairs), 5 to 40 clones per sample, and the supporting Western (23 kDa band in lung) uses a pan-SPANX-N antibody. Consistent with the low bulk values already in the catalog (0.8 TPM duodenum), so this is low-level expression, not a strong off-target signal.
criteria_gap: Consistent with the low values already in the CSV (0.8 TPM duodenum) but the paper frames it as genuine somatic expression rather than noise; not literature-reviewed.

claim: Human: RT-PCR found human SULT6B1 specifically expressed in kidney and testis (mouse and human cloning paper); UniProt curates the same tissue specificity.
verify_reason: PMID 19505954 exists; the abstract states that by RT-PCR 'human SULT6B1 was specifically expressed in kidney and testis', and UniProt Q6IMI4 curates the same with that citation. Caveats: single non-quantitative RT-PCR report, RNA only, tissue source and donor details not in the abstract, and no protein or functional evidence in human kidney.
criteria_gap: The CSV's highest off-target tissue is blood at 1.6 TPM; a gene-specific RT-PCR points at kidney, which bulk thresholds pass. Kidney is in the rare-cell screen, which reported below_screen, so the signal is likely low or confined to a rare cell type.

claim: Human: UniProt P59826 records BPIFB3 as detected in nasal septal epithelium (Bingle and Craven 2002). RNA-seq of human olfactory epithelium against 16 control tissues found BPI-fold proteins, together with lipocalins, to be the most over-expressed non-receptor gene families.
best_source: PMID 27515280, Additional files 2 and 3 (12864_2016_2960_MOESM2_ESM.xlsx, MOESM3_ESM.xlsx); UniProt P59826
verify_reason: UniProt P59826 does carry 'Detected in nasal septal epithelium' with experimental evidence from PMID 11971875. That paper's full text is paywalled; its abstract is family-level only. I opened the per-gene supplementary tables of Olender 2016, which the original researcher had not: BPIFB3 is 648, 333, 242 and 1234 FPKM in the four human olfactory epithelium samples, 0.06 in respiratory epithelium, and at the 0.003 floor in nearly all 16 control tissues (testes 0.14). Fold change is about 49,000 and it is in the 194-gene overexpressed list. Samples were biopsies and autopsies from elective-surgery donors; ages are not stated and respiratory contamination is variable. The paralogs are separate rows with different profiles, so this is gene-level RNA-seq.
criteria_gap: Olfactory and nasal epithelium are absent from the HPA/GTEx bulk panels and from the rare-cell screen tissues, so the highest off-target value (1.26 TPM pituitary) misses the main expression site. The Olender abstract names the family, not the gene; the per-gene table was not opened.

tissue: nasal mucosa, salivary gland, lachrymal gland, lung, liver
cell_type: secretory epithelium (not specified in the UniProt entry)
claim: Human OBP2A is a secreted odorant-binding lipocalin. UniProt (Q9NY56) curates it as strongly expressed in nasal structures, salivary and lachrymal glands and lung (PMID 10607840), and expressed in liver (PMID 27827363).
best_source: PMID 10607840 (DOI 10.1093/hmg/9.2.289) for nasal/salivary/lachrymal/lung; PMID 27827363 (PMC5105165) for liver, weak
verify_reason: UniProt Q9NY56 TISSUE SPECIFICITY reads exactly as claimed. The PMID 10607840 abstract (Lacazette 2000, Hum Mol Genet) states hOBP(IIa) was strongly expressed in nasal structures, salivary and lachrymal glands and lung, and explicitly separates it from the 95%-identical hOBP(IIb) (prostate/mammary profile), so the nasal/salivary/lachrymal/lung part is gene-specific by the authors' account. Caveats: only the abstract was read, so the method and the donor age/normality of the tissues were not checked; both genes were also expressed in vas deferens and placenta. The liver part is weak: PMID 27827363 is a TSC22D4 diabetes paper that measured human OBP2A (LCN13) with a single TaqMan assay (Hs01062934_g1) in patient liver biopsies; specificity against OBP2B was not shown and the tissue is not from healthy donors. HPA's cross-reference in the same UniProt entry says 'Tissue enriched (fallopian)', which does not support lung or salivary expression.
criteria_gap: Nasal/olfactory mucosa and lachrymal gland are not in the bulk panels or the rare-cell screen. Salivary gland and lung are in the panels but show low values (max 2.69 TPM, in skin), so the gene-specific reports contradict the atlases; the label is also flagged mapping_risk (OBP2A/OBP2B paralogs). No literature review exists for it.

claim: Human: a Respiratory Research 2011 study of upper airway tissue reports that secretoglobins including SCGB1C1 (RYD5) are expressed in nasal mucosa and are differentially regulated by inflammatory cytokines.
source: DOI 10.1186/1465-9921-12-28; known only from search-result summary, the PDF was behind a redirect and not read
verify_reason: Full text read (Lu et al., Respir Res 2011, PMID 21385388, PMC3063214). SCGB1C1 mRNA was detected by quantitative RT-PCR with gene-specific primers (NM_145651), and PCR product identity was confirmed by DNA sequencing, in inferior turbinate mucosa from patients having septal surgery with no sinus disease or allergic rhinitis. In explant culture IL-4 and IL-13 up-regulated and IFN-gamma down-regulated it; it was also increased in nasal polyp tissue. Caveats: RNA only, relative quantification so absolute level is unknown, no protein or cell localisation (authors note no antibody was available), and the authors say this was the first demonstration in human airway mucosa. Donor ages were not checked.
criteria_gap: Nasal mucosa is not in the bulk tissue panels or the rare-cell screen, and cytokine-regulated expression would not show in resting tissue.

cell_type: neurons (inferred from the mouse overexpression model, not shown for endogenous human protein)
claim: Human: Letronne et al. 2016 (EBioMedicine, PMID 27333034) report from brain transcriptomics that ADAM30 expression is about 50% lower in Alzheimer's disease brains and inversely correlates with amyloid load, which implies measurable ADAM30 mRNA in non-diseased adult brain. The functional work (cathepsin D activation, APP lysosomal sorting) used neuronal overexpression in mice and cells.
verify_reason: Letronne et al. 2016 (PMID 27333034, full text PMC4972530) says what is claimed, and the full text is stronger than the abstract. ADAM30 mRNA was measured in human frontal cortex on a custom oligonucleotide array (12 AD cases, 12 controls) and validated with a Quantigene probe assay (51 AD, 42 controls), showing about 50% lower expression in AD and an inverse correlation with amyloid load. The paper also reports neuronal immunostaining for ADAM30 in human frontal cortex (Brodmann area 10) with a polyclonal antibody; the claim listed neurons as inferred only from the mouse model. Caveats: values are arbitrary units normalised to housekeeping genes, so the absolute level is unknown and may be very low, consistent with near-zero atlas values; controls are aged post-mortem brains; antibody validation was not checked; and the paper notes ADAM30 is not expressed in mouse brain.
criteria_gap: Catalog shows 0.24 TPM (blood) and 0.0 nTPM, i.e. no brain signal in the atlases, while a targeted study reports quantifiable brain expression. The abstract was read only as quoted in search results (the PubMed page did not load), and absolute expression levels are unknown; could be very low.

claim: Human: UniProt (A8MW95) curates Beclin 2 as present in fetal and adult brain at protein level, citing He et al. 2013, even though the catalog shows 0.0 TPM off-target.
verify_reason: UniProt A8MW95 carries 'Present in fetal and adult brain (at protein level)' with experimental evidence from PMID 23954414. The full text (PMC4231430, Fig. 1C) shows a western blot of human Beclin 2 in fetal and adult human brain lysates. The antibody was raised against Beclin 2 residues 49-67, and siRNA against beclin 2 reduced the band without affecting Beclin 1. Caveats: it is a single western blot from one lab with a custom peptide antibody, with no independent replication found and no cell-type resolution. The mRNA tissue panel in the paper (Fig. 1B) is mouse, not human.
criteria_gap: Bulk RNA and nTPM are 0 and the gene is below the rare-cell screen, so protein-level evidence in adult brain is invisible. BECN2 is intronless, which may also depress RNA-seq quantification.

cell_type: corneal epithelium and endothelium, perivascular cells of iris and retina, intrinsic choroidal neurons
claim: Alarin, a peptide made from a GALP splice variant lacking exon 3, shows immunoreactivity in human corneal epithelium and endothelium, around iris and retinal blood vessels and in intrinsic choroidal neurons; quantitative RT-PCR confirmed alarin mRNA in human retina and choroid. Reviews also place alarin around blood vessels in human and mouse skin.
verify_reason: Abstract of PMID 23178871 read: alarin-like immunoreactivity in human corneal epithelium and endothelium, around iris and retinal blood vessels and in intrinsic choroidal neurons, with quantitative RT-PCR confirming alarin mRNA in human retina and choroid. Caveats: the abstract does not state donor age or health (normal adult donor eyes are assumed, not verified); the authors call it 'alarin-like' immunoreactivity, so antibody specificity is not established beyond the qPCR in retina and choroid; cornea and iris are antibody-only. Alarin is a GALP splice product, so this is the GALP gene and not a paralog, but it bears on only the shared N-terminal residues of the GALP peptide. The skin statement comes from reviews and was not checked.
criteria_gap: Gene-level TPM does not separate the alarin splice variant, cornea and choroid are not in the bulk panels, and antibody evidence for alarin is outside HPA IHC. Note that alarin shares only the first 5 mature-peptide residues with GALP, so the relevance depends on which part of the GALP protein is targeted.

tissue: dorsal root ganglion / trigeminal ganglion (peripheral sensory neurons)
claim: Human: qPCR of whole thoracolumbar DRG from 4 donors showed abundant MRGPRX1, and single-cell RT-PCR detected it in about 79% of 85 picked human DRG neurons (about 99% of those co-expressing TRPV1). Cultured human DRG neurons gave calcium responses to the MRGPRX1 agonists BAM8-22 (about 34% of neurons) and chloroquine (about 10%); MRGPRX1 was not detected in human colon biopsies.
source: PMID 31536477 (JCI Insight 2019;4(20):e131712, doi:10.1172/jci.insight.131712; read as PMC6824308)
best_source: PMID 31536477 (PMC6824308), Results section 'Human DRG neurons express TGR5 and MrgprX1', Figures 11-12; also PMID 11850634 (Nat Neurosci 2002;5:201)
verify_reason: Opened PMC6824308 (Castro et al., JCI Insight 2019, PMID 31536477). The text matches the claim: MrgprX1 absent in colonic biopsies from 15 healthy subjects; qPCR of T9-L1 whole thoracolumbar DRG from 4 human donors showed TGR5 with greater abundance of MrgprX1; single-cell RT-PCR of 85 human DRG neurons, 79% MrgprX1-positive, 99% of those co-expressing TRPV1; calcium imaging responses to BAM8-22 (34%) and chloroquine (10%). Caveats: the paper is mainly a mouse study with human DRG as one results section; the 85 picked neurons were predominantly small-diameter, so 79% is not a whole-ganglion prevalence; donor age and primer specificity against MRGPRX2-4 were not checked in the methods (tissue is organ-donor DRG, assumed adult). Independent support from Lembo et al. 2002 (PMID 11850634), which localised the family to human small sensory neurons.
criteria_gap: Peripheral sensory ganglia (DRG, trigeminal) are in neither the HPA/GTEx bulk panels nor the rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut), so a gene confined to nociceptors reads as near zero (0.1 TPM, basal ganglia) and status is below_screen. Targeting it risks sensory neuron toxicity (itch/pain neuropathy).

claim: Human: UniProt curates MRGPRX1 as a GPCR of small-diameter dorsal root and trigeminal ganglion sensory neurons mediating itch and pain (activated by enkephalin-derived peptides such as BAM8-22 and by chloroquine; Gq coupling sensitises TRPV1). This is a second, curated source for the same function as the primary paper above, not an additional tissue.
source: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q96LB2 (UniProt Q96LB2, function and tissue-specificity fields, fetched via the UniProt REST search)
best_source: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q96LB2 ; underlying primary PMID 11850634 (Lembo et al., Nat Neurosci 2002)
verify_reason: Fetched UniProt Q96LB2. Function field: GPCR 'specifically expressed in sensory neurons of dorsal root ganglion', involved in itch perception and pain transmission, activated by BAM22/BAM8-22 and chloroquine, Gq coupling sensitises TRPV1. Tissue-specificity field: 'Specifically expressed in small-diameter sensory neurons of dorsal root ganglion and trigeminal sensory neurons' (experimental evidence, PMID 11850634). The claim is accurate as stated. As it says itself, this is a curated restatement of the same function, not an independent tissue; some functional detail in the entry (nasal sneezing) is by similarity to mouse.
criteria_gap: Same gap: no sensory ganglion tissue in any expression source used; the literature review covered only about 99 proteins and did not include this one (literature_verdict empty).

tissue: brain (midbrain: substantia nigra, ventral tegmental area)
cell_type: tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons; GAD-positive neurons in substantia nigra pars reticulata
claim: Human: SRY immunoreactivity was detected in adult male (not female) substantia nigra pars compacta within a subpopulation of TH-positive neurons, and in VTA and pars reticulata neurons. In human cell lines SRY knockdown reduced TH, DDC, DBH and MAO-A, so the authors propose it positively regulates catecholamine synthesis in the male midbrain; UniProt also annotates a role in maintaining motor function of dopaminergic neurons (by similarity to rat).
source: PMID 22568433 (Czech et al., J Neurochem 2012); UniProt Q05066
best_source: PMID 22568433 (PMC3529967), Czech et al., J Neurochem 2012
verify_reason: Source exists and says what is claimed. PubMed abstract of PMID 22568433 (Czech et al., J Neurochem 2012;122:260-71): SRY immunoreactivity in human male but not female SNc within a subpopulation of TH-positive neurons, co-localisation with TH in VTA and with GAD in SNr; SRY knockdown in M17 cells reduced TH, DDC, DBH, MAO-A. Full text (PMC3529967): post-mortem brains from 7 donors listed as 'Control' (5 male aged 48-69, 2 female), 43% (+/-9%) of male SNc TH+ neurons SRY-positive; VTA is from a single male. SRY is single-copy and Y-linked, and absence of signal in female SNc argues against cross-reaction with autosomal/X SOX proteins, so the assay is reasonably gene-specific. Caveats that keep this from being strong: one laboratory, one sheep polyclonal antibody (C-terminal peptide aa 189-204), only 2 female negative controls, no peptide block, no western blot and no SRY mRNA (RT-PCR/ISH) on the human brain tissue; the antibody was validated by siRNA/overexpression only in cell lines, and the authors themselves say further studies are required. The functional evidence is cell-line only, and the UniProt motor-function annotation is by similarity to rat. So: expression claim confirmed at antibody level in adult human normal brain; a required function in human is not shown.
criteria_gap: Bulk brain-subregion RNA shows only 1.7 TPM (top tissue skin) and the rare-cell screen is below threshold; expression is confined to a subpopulation of midbrain dopamine neurons in males, so it is diluted in bulk and sex-averaged panels, and the evidence is antibody-level protein that the RNA atlases do not capture. Literature review did not cover this gene.

cell_type: sebaceous gland cells (per HPA cell-type enrichment); keratinization cluster
claim: Human: HPA classes AADACL3 as tissue enhanced in placenta and skin and places it in the 'Skin - Keratinization' expression cluster; a search snippet of the HPA summary also lists sebaceous gland cells as an enriched cell type. No protein data (IHC pending, mass spec not detected) and no functional study.
verify_reason: The HPA pages say what is claimed: RNA tissue specificity is tissue enhanced (placenta, skin), Tau 0.97, expression cluster Skin - Keratinization. The sebaceous detail the original researcher could not see is on the HPA gene summary page, which lists bulk-deconvolution cell type enrichment in skin sebaceous gland cells (plus testis early and late spermatids). Single-cell specificity is extravillous trophoblasts only. There is no protein evidence: IHC is pending and mass spec is not detected. This is atlas RNA only, at low level (1.4 TPM in the catalog), with no independent gene-specific assay or functional study, so it is confirmed only as the weak atlas-level observation it was stated to be.
criteria_gap: The CSV already shows skin as the top off-target tissue at 1.4 TPM; what the number hides is that the signal may be concentrated in a small skin compartment (sebaceous gland or upper epidermis). Skin is not covered by the donor-level rare-cell screen. The sebaceous detail was not on the page I opened.

claim: Human: the cloning paper (Jonsson 2004, Genomics 84:859-866, 'Hash4, a novel human achaete-scute homologue found in fetal skin') found Hash4/ASCL4 expression restricted to skin by real-time PCR, about 7-fold higher in fetal than adult skin, so adult skin is positive at a lower level. UniProt-derived text adds weak expression in adult stomach, kidney, ovary and breast. A mouse review states Ascl4-null mice have no overt phenotype.
source: https://www.genecards.org/card/ASCL4 and https://bvbvf1.bib-bvb.de/vufind/PrimoRecord/cdi_proquest_miscellaneous_66960545 (abstract of Jonsson et al. 2004, read via search results only; PMID not confirmed)
best_source: PMID 15475265 (Jonsson et al. 2004, Genomics 84:859-866); UniProt Q6XD76 tissue specificity
verify_reason: Jonsson et al. 2004 (Genomics 84:859-866) is PMID 15475265. The PubMed abstract says Hash4 expression was restricted to skin among the tissues and cells tested by RT-PCR, with about 7-fold higher expression in fetal than adult skin by real-time PCR, so adult skin is positive at a lower level. UniProt Q6XD76, citing the same paper, reads: expressed in skin, 7-fold higher in fetal than adult skin, weak expression also in fetal lung, aorta and brain and in adult stomach, kidney, ovary and breast. The assay is gene-specific PCR on human tissue. Caveats: no absolute adult level is given, the full text was not opened so the provenance and normality of the adult skin RNA is unchecked, and the mouse Ascl4-null statement was not verified.
criteria_gap: The catalog's top off-target tissue is blood at 1.0 TPM; a gene-specific qPCR report of adult skin expression is not reflected. Likely confined to a minor skin cell population diluted in bulk skin, and skin is not in the rare-cell screen.

claim: Human: OR51A7 (with OR51E2) expression in eccrine sweat glands was confirmed by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry; the ligand beta-ionone activates G-proteins through OR51A7 and topical beta-ionone altered sweating in volunteers (Murayama et al. 2023).
best_source: PMID 37533582 (Murayama et al., JID Innov 2023; PMC10392076)
verify_reason: Full text (PMC10392076) supports the claim as stated. OR51A7 was higher in hidrotic than anhidrotic laser-microdissected sweat glands from anhidrosis (AIGA) patients by RNA-seq. In situ hybridisation with an OR51A7 antisense oligo probe (sense-probe negative control) detected mRNA in acinar and myoepithelial cells of eccrine glands in AIGA sweating areas and in a healthy donor. IHC detected protein in glands of AIGA patients and a healthy donor. Beta-ionone activated G-proteins through OR51A7 in transfected HEK293T cells (minimum dose 100 uM), and topical beta-ionone changed sweating in volunteers in a sex-dependent way. Caveats that limit weight: normal-tissue evidence is a single healthy donor; the IHC antibody is a commercial Invitrogen antibody with no knockout or peptide-block validation (only a no-primary control, data not shown); the ISH probe is one 42-mer with no test against OR51 paralogs; the functional link is overexpression plus a topical test that cannot attribute the effect to OR51A7 rather than OR51E2. Single lab, not replicated.
criteria_gap: Sweat glands are a tiny fraction of bulk skin RNA and skin is not in the donor-level rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut), so the gene stays below_screen at 0.09 TPM. Gene-specific ISH and IHC contradict the atlas zero.

cell_type: melanocytes (sun-damaged skin); stromal cells in scars
claim: Human: nuclear PRAME staining in non-neoplastic skin is usually absent or limited to a few scattered melanocytes, most often in actinically damaged skin; the authors also note occasional weak nuclear staining of stromal cells in scars. This fits the catalog's existing dismissed rare-cell hit in eye melanocytes and hints at damage- or wound-associated expression.
verify_reason: Lezcano 2021 says it as claimed: in non-neoplastic skin nuclear PRAME staining is 'usually absent' or 'limited to few scattered melanocytes most frequently encountered in actinically damaged skin', and 'occasional weak nuclear immunoreactivity of stromal cells in scars'. This is the nuclear pattern with the diagnostic antibody, in human non-neoplastic tissue. Caveats: it is a review reporting the authors' observations without counts; the tissue is damaged or scarred rather than strictly normal; and the larger 2022 IHC study found all cutaneous structures other than sebaceous glands negative. So it is real but rare, focal and weak. The link to the catalog's eye-melanocyte hit is the flagger's inference, not in the source.
criteria_gap: Scattered single cells and damage- or scar-associated expression are invisible to bulk RNA, and skin is not in the rare-cell screen. The melanocyte hit was dismissed as conflicting_or_nonspecific, but protein-level data agree with it.

claim: Human: immunohistochemistry with TCHHL1 antibodies shows protein in the basal layer of normal epidermis and in cultured growing keratinocytes, with mRNA detected in normal skin and cultured keratinocytes.
verify_reason: PMID 23376073 (Yamakoshi et al., BBRC 2013) exists and its abstract says this directly: antibodies raised against the TCHHL1 C-terminus stained the basal layer of normal human epidermis and the perinuclear area of cultured growing keratinocytes, and TCHHL1 mRNA was detected in normal skin and cultured keratinocytes. The C-terminal immunogen makes cross-reaction with other fused S100 proteins (TCHH, hornerin, filaggrin) less likely. Caveats: abstract only was read; a single laboratory with an in-house polyclonal antibody; no knockout or peptide-block validation is mentioned in the abstract; donor age is not stated.
criteria_gap: Bulk skin RNA is only 0.7 TPM and the rare-cell screen does not cover skin, so a protein restricted to the basal keratinocyte layer is below every threshold; skin is a vital, non-disposable tissue.

tissue: olfactory epithelium, tongue, minor salivary gland
claim: Human: a 2025 preprint, citing the human olfactory transcriptome study, lists BPIFB6 with BPIFB3 and BPIFB4 among the most tissue-enriched, highly expressed genes in olfactory epithelium. Olender et al. state in their abstract that BPI-fold proteins show the highest over-expression there. UniProt Q8NFQ5 records only tonsil expression.
verify_reason: The cited preprint returned HTTP 403. Its published version (Cells 2025, PMID 41369347, PMC12691349) lists BPIFB6 only in a sequence-identity table and names BPIFB3 and BPIFB4, not BPIFB6, as olfactory-expressed. The claim is nonetheless supported by the Olender 2016 supplementary tables: BPIFB6 is in the overexpressed gene list with fold change about 9,000, at 9.9, 5.0, 6.8 and 224 FPKM in the four human olfactory samples, 0.07 in respiratory epithelium and about 0.003-0.03 in controls. 'Highly expressed' is overstated: three of four samples are 5-10 FPKM and one is 224, well below BPIFB3 and BPIFB4. Donor ages are not stated. Only olfactory epithelium is supported; no source was found for tongue or minor salivary gland, and UniProt Q8NFQ5 records tonsil only.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is not in any panel the screen uses; the 2.6 TPM salivary gland value is probably a diluted signal from the same secretory lineage. The gene-level claim is secondhand (preprint seen only as a search-result summary; Olender abstract names the family only).

claim: Human: UniProt Q5QGT7 curates RTP2 as expressed in circumvallate papillae and testis, citing PMID 16720576.
source: UniProt Q5QGT7 (https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q5QGT7), citing PMID 16720576; the primary paper was not opened
best_source: PMID 16720576 (DOI 10.1074/jbc.M513637200), abstract only; UniProt Q5QGT7 and the RTP1 entry for the per-gene contrast
verify_reason: UniProt Q5QGT7 does state 'Expressed in circumvallate papillae and testis' with experimental evidence from PMID 16720576 (Behrens et al., JBC 2006). The curation is per gene: the same paper gives RTP1 'Expressed in testis' only, so RTP2 is distinguished from its closest paralog. The abstract confirms human circumvallate papillae and testis were assayed. Caveats: I could not open the full text (publisher returned 403), so the assay type, band strength and donor age are unverified; it is a single RNA-level study with no protein data, and HPA bulk shows RTP2 only at about 1-2 nTPM in skeletal muscle and testis.
criteria_gap: Taste papillae are not sampled as a distinct tissue in bulk panels or in the rare-cell screen; a bulk tongue sample would dilute the signal.

claim: Human: UniProt curates expression in taste receptor cells of the tongue and palate epithelia, exclusively in gustducin-positive cells, with a possible role sensing gastrointestinal contents.
best_source: PMID 18003842 (Behrens et al. 2007, J Neurosci); UniProt Q9NYW7
verify_reason: UniProt Q9NYW7 carries the quoted tissue-specificity and function text, but with no evidence code or citation (it traces to rodent-era in situ work). A stronger human source exists: Behrens et al. 2007 showed all 25 human TAS2R genes expressed in taste receptor cells of human circumvallate papillae by in situ hybridisation with gene-specific probes. The gastrointestinal-sensing role in UniProt is speculative ('may').
criteria_gap: Taste epithelium is absent from the HPA/GTEx bulk panels and from the rare-cell screen tissues.
