It reports a CABS1-immunoreactive 27 kDa band in saliva of all volunteers, acute stress increasing the 18, 27 and 55 kDa bands, and changes in the 27 kDa band positively associated with salivary cortisol in both acute and academic stress. So the claim matches. Weakened because the evidence is an immunoreactive band only, and the same group's 2024 paper states they are 'unable to confirm the presence of a relatively abundant 27 kDa CABS1 form in human saliva'. The stress-induced form is therefore not established as CABS1. It is also a secreted fluid, not a tissue of expression.
criteria_gap: Stress-induced or secreted protein forms are invisible to constitutive bulk and single-cell RNA atlases.

cell_type: pyloric gland epithelium; more frequent with intestinal metaplasia
claim: Human: CT83 (KK-LC-1) mRNA was detected by RT-PCR in 7% of stomachs without gastric cancer (115 non-GC patients), and every positive case carried Helicobacter pylori; in stomachs with a tumor, 77% of non-tumor sites were positive. A companion study (PMID 29666402) localised the non-tumor signal to pyloric glands of the lower corpus (59% of pyloric-gland samples, none in fundic glands).
verify_reason: Both sources exist and the numbers match: PMID 36484013 abstract gives 77% of non-tumor sites in tumor-bearing stomachs vs 7% in stomachs without tumors (118 GC, 115 non-GC patients), all positives H. pylori carriers; PMC5904109 full text gives 45/76 (59.2%) pyloric gland samples and 0/13 fundic, 76.6% in lower-corpus pyloric glands. CT83 is single-copy so RT-PCR is gene-specific. But the tissue is not normal: all positives are H. pylori-infected, atrophic/metaplastic or tumor-adjacent mucosa (the authors call it a pre-cancerous marker), and 93% of cancer-free stomachs were negative. Assay is 40-cycle end-point RT-PCR with gel readout, mRNA only, no protein in non-tumor tissue, one research group. Field cancerization is an alternative explanation. Real as a disease-state/induced signal, not as healthy-tissue expression.
criteria_gap: Expression is induced by infection/atrophic or pre-malignant change in non-cancerous gastric mucosa, so healthy-donor bulk RNA (HPA/GTEx), HPA single-cell clusters and the rare-cell screen do not see it. Evidence is 40-cycle end-point RT-PCR from one research group, with no protein confirmation in cancer-free stomachs.

claim: Human: the Human Protein Atlas reports IHC staining (antibody HPA043787) in cilia of respiratory epithelium and fallopian tube as well as seminiferous ducts, although RNA is 'not detected'. The antibody may cross-react with the paralog DCAF8.
verify_reason: The HPA page does state 'Expression in cilia in seminiferous ducts, fallopian tube and respiratory epithelium', with antibody HPA043787, RNA tissue specificity 'Not detected', and an IHC reliability score of 'Enhanced' (stronger than the claim implied). It rests on one antibody, RNA is absent in the stained tissue, and DCAF8L1 belongs to the DCAF8 family (DCAF8 is broadly expressed), so cross-reactivity is not excluded; I did not check the antigen sequence against the paralogs.
criteria_gap: This is protein-level staining in airway cilia despite 0.05 TPM RNA. An RNA-driven screen ignores it, and the catalog's IHC check may not have counted it.

claim: Human: DCST1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that negatively regulates type I interferon signalling by ubiquitinating STAT2 for degradation (Nair et al. 2016). UniProt records it as induced by IFNB1. The work was done in cell lines and gives no normal-tissue expression data.
verify_reason: The source exists and says this: Nair et al. 2016 (full text read via Europe PMC) show DCST1 interacts with STAT2 and promotes its K48 ubiquitination and degradation, and that DCST1 mRNA and protein are upregulated by IFN-beta. UniProt Q5T197 carries 'INDUCTION: Induced by IFNB1'. All of it was done in HEK293T cells, largely with ectopic expression plus siRNA; there is no normal-tissue or primary-cell data, so it does not show expression in any normal adult tissue.
criteria_gap: Interferon-induced expression would not appear in resting-tissue atlases. The catalog already shows 3.6 TPM in skin and a dismissed retinal cone hit, so a somatic role beyond sperm-egg fusion is plausible.

claim: Human: DEFB108 mRNA is not constitutive but was induced in gingival keratinocytes by IL-1beta and Candida, with synergy when IL-1beta was combined with TNF-alpha or IFN-gamma. The RT-PCR may not distinguish DEFB108B from its paralog copies.
verify_reason: The abstract of PMID 14871351 confirms 'DEFB-108 and 114 were induced by interleukin (IL)-1beta and Candida species' with synergism for DEFB-108 when IL-1beta was combined with TNF-alpha or IFN-gamma. The source is real and says this, but it reports 'DEFB-108' without separating DEFB108B from the other DEFB108 copies in the 8p23 cluster, and the result is from stimulated cultured keratinocytes, not tissue. Abstract only.
criteria_gap: This is inflammation-induced expression in an epithelium absent from all panels. Steady-state atlases of healthy tissue cannot see it.

claim: Human: UniProt's tissue-specificity annotation states MBD3L2 is detected at low levels in several somatic tissues (and at high levels in the PA-1 ovarian teratocarcinoma line), in contrast to the catalog's 0.0 off-target TPM. The specific tissues and the underlying paper were not retrieved in this session.
best_source: PMID 12504854 (Jiang et al., Genomics 2002) and PMID 15701600 (Jin et al., J Biol Chem 2005), abstracts only; via https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8NHZ7
verify_reason: UniProt Q8NHZ7 tissue-specificity field does read 'Detected at low levels in several somatic tissues (PubMed:12504854, PubMed:15701600). Highly expressed in the ovarian teratocarcinoma cell line PA-1'. The abstracts of both underlying papers were read: Jiang et al. 2002 (Genomics 80:621) says only 'Expression of MBD3L2 was found in germ cell tumors and some somatic tissues'; Jin et al. 2005 (JBC 280:12700) says 'MBD3L2 expression is more widespread' than MBD3L1. Neither abstract names the tissues, their adult/normal status, or the level; full texts were not opened. The 2002-2005 RT-PCR predates annotation of the near-identical copies MBD3L2B/3/4/5, so it is unlikely to distinguish MBD3L2 from them (my inference, primers not checked). Real but low-level, unspecified and paralog-ambiguous.
criteria_gap: Bulk RNA reads 0.0 TPM and the group is flagged mapping_risk=True (near-identical MBD3L2/2B/3/4/5 copies), so multi-mapping reads may be discarded and low somatic expression seen by gene-specific RT-PCR would be invisible. Low-confidence: curated one-line annotation only. NOTE on coverage of this batch: the session's shared web-search budget ran out after two searches, so MAS1L, MPC1L, MROH2B, MINDY4B, MEIOSIN, MOS and the MAGE/MBD3L genes were checked only against UniProt curated fields (function, tissue specificity, induction, disease), which showed no non-reproductive role; they did not get a literature search and absence of findings for them is weaker than for a fully searched gene.

claim: Human: functional OR1A2 was reported at mRNA and protein level (RT-PCR, immunostaining, Western blot, Ca2+ imaging) in primary alveolar macrophages from bronchoalveolar lavage, where its activation modulated cytokine release and phagocytosis. The cells came from 50 patients with pulmonary disease, not healthy donors.
best_source: PMID 36503361 (Weidinger et al. 2022, Mol Med; PMC9743598)
verify_reason: Source exists and matches the claim (full text opened). All BAL donors were pulmonary-disease patients (COPD, ILD, pneumonia, lung cancer, asthma); no healthy controls for OR1A2. RT-PCR used OR1A2 primers with a no-RT control and OR1A1 was RT-PCR negative, which partly supports gene specificity, but no amplicon sequencing, no knockdown or antagonist; antibodies validated only by heterologous overexpression, and citronellal also activates OR1A1 so function is not gene-specific. Abstract says 50 patients, Methods 49. Disease-state cells, so not normal-tissue evidence.
criteria_gap: Sorted immune cells in the screen are blood-derived, so tissue-resident alveolar macrophages are not specifically sampled, and expression may be disease- or activation-induced. The CSV shows only 0.25 TPM in blood. Rated possible because donors were diseased and only the abstract was read.

cell_type: pulmonary artery smooth muscle and endothelial cells
claim: Human cells in vitro, with a mouse hypoxia model: OR1N1 was identified as a RELM-beta binding partner by affinity purification-mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation, and siRNA silencing of OR1N1 reduced viability of human pulmonary artery smooth muscle and endothelial cells.
source: PMID 41317264 (Lin et al. 2026, Cardiovasc Drugs Ther)
best_source: PMID 41317264 (Lin et al. 2026, Cardiovasc Drugs Ther; PMC13388652)
verify_reason: Source exists and abstract matches the claim, but full text shows the evidence does not establish endogenous expression in normal human pulmonary vascular cells: AP-MS and co-IP were done in MRC-5 fetal lung fibroblasts with transfected Flag-tagged constructs (tag-based detection, no OR1N1 antibody), OR1N1 mRNA was shown in hypoxia-PH mouse lung and in RELM-beta-overexpressing PASMCs (induced, not baseline), knockdown shown only at mRNA level, and the viability effect is relative to a RELM-beta overexpression group. No Western, IHC or baseline qPCR in normal human lung. The in vivo confirmation used GIPC1 and CLIC4 knockouts, not OR1N1. Cultured cells in an artificial overexpression system; siRNA off-target effects not excluded.
criteria_gap: The CSV shows 1.0 TPM in blood and nothing in lung. A knockdown phenotype implies functional protein in pulmonary vascular cells, which bulk RNA thresholds would not flag. Single study in cultured cells, abstract only, donor status not stated.

cell_type: airway smooth muscle cells (also respiratory epithelium and submucosal cells by IHC)
claim: Human: OR2AG1 was detected in primary airway smooth muscle cells from three donors (tumor-free bronchial tissue from lung-resection patients) by RT-PCR, immunocytochemistry and Western blot, and IHC on human lung stained smooth muscle and respiratory epithelium. Its agonist amyl butyrate evoked cAMP-dependent Ca2+ signals and reduced histamine-induced contraction.
source: PMID 27540365 (Kalbe et al. 2016, Front Physiol; PMC4972829)
best_source: PMID 27540365 (Kalbe et al. 2016, Front Physiol; PMC4972829)
verify_reason: Source exists and says what is claimed (full text opened: OR1D2 and OR2AG1 by RT-PCR, ICC, Western blot in HASMCs from three donors, DAB IHC on human lung, amyl butyrate functional effects). Weaknesses: donors were bronchial carcinoma patients (tumor-adjacent 'tumor-free' tissue), cells were cultured; no amplicon sequencing reported; antibody validated only by overexpression in Hana3A cells for ICC with no test against the near-identical paralog OR2AG2 and no knockdown or OR2AG1-specific antagonist; function attributed via a ligand, not genetic evidence. Single lab, unreplicated. Real but weaker than 'documented protein in normal tissue'.
criteria_gap: The CSV maximum is 2.2 TPM in basal ganglia with no lung signal and rare-cell status below_screen. Airway smooth muscle is a minority cell type diluted in bulk lung, so protein-level and functional evidence in a vital tissue is invisible to the RNA thresholds; this gene has no literature verdict. Caveat: single lab, cultured cells, and the antibody was validated only by overexpression.

claim: Human: a common nonsense SNP in OR4X1 (Tyr273Ter) was associated with FEV1/FVC in 2,970 Japanese subjects, and predicted loss-of-function variants in OR4X1 were among 10 genes associated with blood pressure in UK Biobank exomes (n = 454,709). Neither study measured expression; the null allele is common, so the gene is not vital.
best_source: PMID 17964544 and PMID 37451613 (abstracts only; full texts not opened)
verify_reason: Both abstracts exist and say what is claimed: rs10838851 (Tyr273Ter) was associated with FEV1/FVC in 2,970 Japanese subjects (P=0.008, among 7 OR nonsense SNPs tested; about 1 percentage point between genotypes), and OR4X1 is one of 10 genes with single predicted loss-of-function variants associated with blood pressure in UK Biobank exomes (n=454,709). Neither measured expression in any tissue, so there is no evidence of normal adult tissue expression or function. The stop allele is the major haplotype in the Japanese cohort (frequency about 0.67), so loss is tolerated. The lung association is a modest candidate-SNP result that I did not find replicated, and the blood-pressure paper notes its genes map near known GWAS loci, so a common stop variant may simply tag a nearby causal signal. The variant is gene-specific, but the finding does not locate OR4X1 in lung or vessels.
criteria_gap: Genetic association hints at a non-olfactory role that RNA atlases cannot show (0.27 TPM, blood). No tissue or cell type is established, so this is weak evidence against the candidate.

claim: P2Y4-null mice lose UTP/ATP-induced chloride secretion in jejunal epithelium, the first demonstrated physiological role of the receptor; mice are otherwise grossly normal. Mouse data; receptor mRNA was detected in mouse liver, stomach and intestine.
verify_reason: PMID 12644577 says exactly this: P2Y4-null mice lose UTP/ATP-induced jejunal chloride secretion and are otherwise grossly normal, with mRNA loss checked in liver, stomach and intestine. PMID 15718265 adds colonic K+ secretion shared with P2Y2. It is mouse only, and the abstract notes the human receptor differs pharmacologically (UTP only). No human gut expression evidence is cited.
criteria_gap: Functional epithelial receptor at low transcript abundance; the catalog's top off-target is blood at 3.6 TPM and gut was below the rare-cell threshold. Low-copy GPCRs can be functional below the TPM cutoffs.

claim: UniProt notes PASD1 transcripts were found in histologically normal tissues from patients with uterine, lung and small-intestine cancers, while otherwise testis-specific. These are tumor-adjacent samples, so contamination or field effect is likely.
verify_reason: UniProt Q8IV76 does carry the note 'Found in histologically normal tissues from patients with uterus, lung and small intestine cancers', citing PMID 15162151. The abstract of that paper states PASD1 mRNA was restricted to normal testis, with frequent expression in solid tumours. The signal is therefore in tumour-adjacent tissue from cancer patients, not healthy donors, and uterus is a reproductive tissue. Not evidence of normal-tissue expression.
criteria_gap: RT-PCR signal in tumor-adjacent normal tissue is not visible in healthy-donor atlases; weak evidence, flagged only for completeness.

claim: Human: UniProt (Q86YR6, citing PMID 12475935) records POTED expression in normal prostate, in basal and terminal epithelial cells, alongside ovary, testis and placenta. The same source lists POTEC (B2RU33) as expressed in prostate and testis.
verify_reason: UniProt Q86YR6 and Bera 2002 (PMID 12475935, full text opened) do report POTE in normal prostate, with in situ signal in basal and terminal epithelial cells. Two weaknesses. First, the in situ probe was a 1-kb 5' fragment and the paralogs are 90-98% identical, so the cell-type localisation is family-level, not POTED-specific; the dot blot, Northern and 16-tissue PCR were also not paralog-resolved. The only paralog-resolved evidence is cloning and sequencing of prostate and testis cDNA, which found transcripts from chromosomes 2, 14, 15, 21 and 22; chromosome 21 is POTED, so POTED transcription in prostate is supported, but without quantitation. Second, prostate is a male reproductive accessory gland, so this is a finding only if the screen does not exempt prostate. The same paper found no signal in brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, colon, pancreas, spleen, thymus, small intestine or peripheral blood leukocytes, which supports the candidate. Separately, the POTEC (chromosome 18) prostate claim conflicts with the paper, which did not find chromosome 18 transcripts among the sequenced prostate and testis clones.
criteria_gap: Only relevant if prostate is not counted among the exempt reproductive organs. POTE paralogs are flagged mapping_risk, so atlas RNA may under-count them through multi-mapping; the original paper used gene-specific assays. I read the UniProt annotation only.

cell_type: bronchoalveolar / alveolar type II-like epithelial cells (human cell lines)
claim: Human: RBMXL3 was pulled out by proteomics as a protein binding a hairpin element in the surfactant protein B (SFTPB) mRNA 3'UTR, and siRNA against RBMXL3 reduced dexamethasone-induced SP-B mRNA in human bronchoalveolar cells; UniProt curates this as its function. The evidence is from cultured lung epithelial lines (A549 and HEK293 are in the indexing), and the abstract shows no endogenous expression in normal adult lung tissue, so this is a glucocorticoid-dependent, cell-line-level lead only.
source: PMID 33719563 (Am J Physiol Lung Cell Mol Physiol 2021;320:L942-L957), read as the Europe PMC abstract; UniProt Q8N7X1 https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8N7X1.txt
best_source: PMID 33719563, DOI 10.1152/ajplung.00022.2020 (Europe PMC abstract); UniProt Q8N7X1 https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8N7X1.txt (function curated from that paper only; caution note on RBMX retrogene origin; HPA testis-enriched)
verify_reason: The source exists and says what the finding reports: PMID 33719563 (Am J Physiol Lung Cell Mol Physiol 2021, L942-L957) identifies RBMXL3 by proteomics as a protein binding the 30-nt hairpin element in the human SP-B mRNA 3'UTR, and siRNA against RBMXL3 reduced dexamethasone-induced SP-B mRNA in 'human bronchoalveolar cells'. UniProt Q8N7X1 curates this as the function from that single paper. But it is not evidence of expression or function in normal adult human lung. The abstract describes only cultured cells (MeSH indexing lists A549 and HEK293 cells, plus mouse lung epithelial cells in which RBMXL3 was expressed exogenously with a plasmid reporter); it reports no endogenous RBMXL3 RNA or protein in normal lung tissue or primary alveolar type II cells. A549 is a lung adenocarcinoma line, so endogenous expression there is tumor-line expression, which is expected for a cancer/testis gene. UniProt's own cross-reference gives HPA 'Tissue enriched (testis)'. Gene specificity is also unproven from the abstract: UniProt cautions that RBMXL3 is an RBMX-derived retrogene, and neither the proteomic peptide assignment nor the siRNA is shown in the abstract to discriminate it from RBMX or other RBMX-like paralogs. I read only the abstract and the UniProt entry, not the full text, so the paper may contain specificity controls or tissue data I did not see. As it stands this is a single-lab, cell-line, glucocorticoid-dependent mechanistic lead, as the finding itself concedes, and does not show a normal-tissue liability.
criteria_gap: Bulk lung RNA is near zero (catalog peak is 1.3 TPM in hypothalamus) and the rare-cell screen was below threshold, so a functional role in a minority lung cell type under glucocorticoid stimulation would not register. No literature review existed for this gene. RBMXL3 is an intronless RBMX retrogene, so both atlas quantification and siRNA/proteomic specificity against RBMX are uncertain.

claim: Human: UniProt P60153 states RNASE9 is widely expressed at the mRNA level, while the protein is restricted to epididymis and sperm (PMID 18992174, PMID 19137000). The RNA claim contradicts the atlases (0 TPM off-target), but the protein evidence supports restriction.
source: UniProt P60153 (https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P60153), citing PMID 18992174 and PMID 19137000; the primary papers were not opened
best_source: PMID 18992174 / PMC2669477 (the RT-PCR claim); PMID 19137000 and HPA ENSG00000188655 (epididymis-restricted)
verify_reason: UniProt P60153 does say 'At the mRNA level, widely expressed' and the primary paper (Liu et al., BMC Res Notes 2008, PMC2669477, full text read) reports a 550 bp RT-PCR band in epididymis, heart, lung, liver, spleen, kidney, stomach and testis, absent only in muscle. But this is non-quantitative end-point RT-PCR from 2 ug RNA; the passages I read mention no product sequencing, and I did not check the methods for DNase treatment, a no-RT control or donor ages, so a genomic DNA artefact cannot be excluded. The second paper (PMID 19137000) found protein only in epididymis and not in other tissues examined, and HPA shows RNA enriched in epididymis only (93 nTPM, epididymal principal cells). The weight of evidence favours restriction; the wide-RNA claim is a single weak assay.
criteria_gap: Bulk RNA atlases show no off-target expression, whereas a gene-specific RT-PCR study reports wide mRNA expression; the screen has no way to register that conflict. Likely low impact given the epididymis-restricted protein.

claim: Mouse only: Spam1 RNA (RT-PCR, in situ) and protein (Western, IHC) were detected in kidney cortex, mainly proximal tubules and glomeruli, and Spam1-null mice had reduced urine volume and failed to raise urine osmolality after water deprivation. An earlier mouse study also detected PH-20 transcripts in normal kidney and tubular cells. A human Northern of 16 tissues found expression strictly limited to testis (PMID 8575780), so human relevance is unconfirmed.
best_source: PMID 17446714 (Grigorieva 2007, mouse); PMID 8575780 (Jones 1995, human Northern, testis only)
verify_reason: Both mouse sources exist and say what is claimed. PMID 17446714: Spam1 RNA (RT-PCR, in situ) and protein (Western, IHC) in mouse kidney cortex, mainly proximal tubules and glomeruli; Spam1-null mice had reduced urine volume and no rise in urine osmolality after 24 h water deprivation. PMID 9933825: PH-20 transcripts in normal mouse kidney and tubular cells. The null mouse makes it gene-specific, but it is mouse-only. The one human source checked, PMID 8575780, found a single 2.4 kb transcript strictly limited to testis across 16 tissues by Northern, which agrees with the human RNA atlases. No human kidney evidence was found, and Northern would not detect very low expression.
criteria_gap: Human bulk RNA shows only 0.4 TPM (duodenum) and the kidney rare-cell screen is below threshold; the screen has no cross-species knockout or protein evidence layer, and SPAM1 was not literature-reviewed.

tissue: several nongametogenic adult tissues (not named in abstract)
claim: Human: SPANX-N family reported as expressed at a low level in several nongametogenic adult tissues, in contrast to SPANX-A/D. Family-level statement from the abstract; member-specific tissues not verified.
best_source: PMID 17406683 full text, Table 2 and Figure 6b (PMC1831492)
verify_reason: Full text of PMID 17406683 read. By cloned-and-sequenced RT-PCR (Table 2), SPANX-N2 transcripts were found in testis, prostate, cervix and placenta only, all reproductive-tract or placental; lung, colon, brain, liver, muscle, spleen, heart and kidney were negative. The only non-reproductive hint is a Western blot of lung in which a 27 kDa band co-migrates with recombinant SPANX-N2, but the antibody recognises all five SPANX-N proteins equally, so that is not gene-specific and is not backed by N2 RNA in lung. N2 also carries an exon 2 frameshift per the paper.
criteria_gap: Flagged mapping_risk and reads 0.0 TPM off-target; multi-mapping among SPANX-N paralogs could hide the low somatic expression the paper reports.

tissue: several nongametogenic adult tissues (not named in abstract)
claim: Human: SPANX-N family reported as expressed at a low level in several nongametogenic adult tissues, in contrast to SPANX-A/D. Family-level statement from the abstract; member-specific tissues not verified.
verify_reason: Full text of PMID 17406683 read. In Table 2, SPANX-N4 transcripts were found in testis and prostate only; cervix, placenta, lung, colon, brain, liver, muscle, spleen, heart, kidney and lymph node were negative. So the family-level 'several nongametogenic tissues' statement reduces to prostate alone for this member, a male reproductive accessory gland, at roughly 50 to 100 times below testis. Counts as a finding only if prostate is treated as non-reproductive.
criteria_gap: Consistent with the low values already in the CSV (0.5 TPM hippocampal formation) but the paper frames it as genuine somatic expression rather than noise; not literature-reviewed.

tissue: small intestine (ileum); broad tissues in mouse
claim: Mouse: Srm transcripts were described as 'rather ubiquitous' across tissues and the single knockout has no apparent phenotype; triple knockout of Brk/Ptk6, Srms and Frk impairs ileal homeostasis and recovery from radiation-induced mucosal damage, whereas single or double knockouts do not, indicating a redundant epithelial role.
source: PMID 7935409 (Kohmura et al., Mol Cell Biol 1994); PMID 37523817 (Kikuchi et al., BBRC 2023)
best_source: PMID 37523817 (Kikuchi et al., BBRC 2023); PMID 7935409 (Kohmura et al., MCB 1994)
verify_reason: Both sources exist and say what is claimed. PMID 7935409 (Kohmura et al., Mol Cell Biol 1994): mouse Srm, 'expression of two transcripts is rather ubiquitous and changes according to tissue and developmental stage'; knockout mice 'displayed no apparent phenotype'. PMID 37523817 (Kikuchi et al., BBRC 2023): Brk/Ptk6-Srms-Frk triple-knockout mice have reduced ileal stem/progenitor population and defective recovery from radiation-induced mucosal damage; 'single- or double-knockout of BFK genes did not elicit such abnormalities'. The knockouts are gene-targeted so the genetics are gene-specific, but all evidence is mouse; the phenotype requires loss of all three kinases, so it does not show that Srms itself is expressed or needed in ileal epithelium (the triple-KO effect could be carried by Ptk6/Frk, which are the well-established gut epithelial members); the 1994 'ubiquitous' statement is Northern-level and includes developmental stages. No human adult data. Low-priority, as the finding itself concedes.
criteria_gap: The catalog value (4.2 TPM spleen, 0.7 TPM in disposable tissue) sits under the bulk threshold and the gene has no literature verdict; mouse data indicate low but broad somatic expression with a redundant function in gut epithelium regeneration, i.e. an injury-induced context the constitutive RNA screen does not test. Reassuringly the single knockout is benign.

claim: Human: UniProt records conflicting tissue specificity, 'widely expressed' per PubMed:12621555 against testis-specific per PubMed:21711156, with protein shown in sperm. I read the UniProt entry, not the papers; the human disease phenotype is male infertility only (spermatogenic failure 16).
verify_reason: UniProt Q8TC36 records the conflict exactly as stated. PMID 12621555 (2003, Chinese-language cloning paper) does say human TSARG4 mRNA 'is expressed in a wide range of adult tissues, including testis', with no assay detail in the abstract; SUN5 is 45% identical to SPAG4. The abstract of PMID 21711156 only confirms protein in human testis and does not itself state testis specificity. Later protein data (sperm) and the infertility-only loss-of-function phenotype point to a testis-restricted role, so the wide-expression report is most likely superseded.
criteria_gap: An older gene-specific report contradicts the atlases (0.19 TPM maximum); most likely superseded, since the later paper and the loss-of-function phenotype are testis-restricted.

claim: Human: duodenal L cells express sweet taste receptors, alpha-gustducin and other taste signalling elements; in the human L-cell line NCI-H716, sugar- and sucralose-driven GLP-1 release was blocked by the sweet receptor antagonist lactisole. The abstract says 'sweet taste receptors' (T1R2/T1R3 heterodimer) rather than naming TAS1R2 alone.
best_source: PMID 17724330; UniProt Q8TE23 for taste function
verify_reason: PMID 17724330 exists and the abstract says human duodenal L cells express 'sweet taste receptors', gustducin and other taste elements, and that lactisole blocked GLP-1 release in NCI-H716 cells. The abstract does not name TAS1R2; lactisole acts on TAS1R3, so the functional block is not TAS1R2-specific, the function is in a tumour-derived cell line, and the tissue evidence is antibody staining. Abstract only read. Taste-bud function with TAS1R3 is well established (UniProt Q8TE23) but UniProt has no tissue-specificity entry.
criteria_gap: Rare endocrine cell in gut; CSV shows below_screen for rare cells and 0.22 TPM bulk (skin), so a sparse L-cell signal would be diluted. Taste buds, the primary site (UniProt function: sweet receptor with TAS1R3), are absent from all panels.

claim: Human: in HGF-1 gingival fibroblasts, TAS2R50 transcript was regulated (RT-qPCR) and siRNA knockdown of TAS2R50 altered the trans-resveratrol effect on IL-6 release. Cell-line evidence only.
verify_reason: PMID 33461297 exists and its title states TAS2R50 mediates the resveratrol effect on IL-6 release in HGF-1 cells; the abstract reports RT-qPCR regulation of TAS2R50 and a TAS2R50 siRNA knockdown. It is gene-specific but entirely a cultured cell line, with no tissue-level expression in gingiva shown. The finding already says this; it stays 'possible' at most. Abstract only read.
criteria_gap: Gingiva/oral mucosa fibroblasts are not in the bulk panels; a cultured line, so only suggestive of in vivo expression.

claim: Human: RT-qPCR on primary lung macrophages measured 16 TAS2Rs; TAS2R7 (and TAS2R38) transcripts increased after LPS stimulation, and TAS2R agonists inhibited cytokine release. Macrophages came from lung resections of carcinoma patients.
verify_reason: PMID 31632299 exists; abstract and full text (PMC6783802) confirm TaqMan RT-qPCR of 16 TAS2Rs including TAS2R7 in human lung macrophages, with a significant LPS-induced increase for TAS2R7 and TAS2R38. Weakened because the macrophages came from lung resections of carcinoma patients (not normal donors), the evidence is transcript only, and the paper's functional conclusion implicates TAS2Rs 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 14, 30, 39 and 40, not TAS2R7, in cytokine inhibition. So induced RNA is real but no TAS2R7 function is shown.
criteria_gap: Induced expression in activated macrophages; resting sorted immune cells and bulk lung RNA would not show an LPS-dependent increase.

claim: Human: UniProt annotates TFDP3 as induced in response to DNA damage, citing a paper on E2F-1 regulation by a DNA damage-responsive DP partner. The evidence is likely from cell lines, so induction in normal tissue is unproven.
verify_reason: UniProt Q5H9I0 does annotate 'INDUCTION: In response to DNA damage' citing PMID 20559320, and that paper (Ingram et al., Cell Death Differ 2011) says DP-4 (= TFDP3) 'is induced in DNA-damaged cells' and that depleting it restores E2F-1 activity, so it is gene-specific. But the abstract refers only to 'cells', which means cultured (almost certainly tumour-derived) lines; there is no evidence of induction in normal adult human tissue. The finding itself conceded this. It stays a hypothesis for normal tissue, not a documented off-target liability.
criteria_gap: The screen measures only constitutive expression; a DNA-damage-inducible gene could switch on in normal tissue under genotoxic stress such as chemotherapy or radiation.

claim: Human TRIM43B is a near-identical paralog of TRIM43, which is induced by DUX4 during herpesvirus infection; the same induction is plausible for TRIM43B but the abstract does not mention it and UniProt A6NCK2 has no annotation. Family-level inference only.
best_source: PMID 30420784 (PMC6294671), methods RNA-seq section; UniProt A6NCK2 (no annotation)
verify_reason: The claim is honestly labelled as a family-level inference, and that is all it is. The abstract of PMID 30420784 does not mention TRIM43B and UniProt A6NCK2 has no induction, tissue or function annotation. The only mention in the full text is one methods sentence: 'the transcripts of the three TRIM43 gene copies found in humans (TRIM43A, TRIM43B and TRIM43C), were analyzed' in the RNA-seq of HSV-1-infected and DUX4-transfected HEK 293T cells. That makes it plausible that TRIM43B reads contribute to the reported induction (and TRIM43B is a known DUX4 target in the FSHD literature), but the paper gives no TRIM43B-specific result, and none of its assays separates the copies. No evidence in normal adult uninfected tissue.
criteria_gap: Same as TRIM43: steady-state atlases cannot show infection-induced expression, and short reads map ambiguously between the two paralogs (mapping_risk is True), so a signal could be assigned to either.

tissue: virus-infected somatic tissue (shown only in the A549 human lung carcinoma line)
cell_type: A549 cells after dsRNA transfection or Rift Valley fever reporter virus infection
claim: Human TRIM48 is described as an induced negative-feedback regulator of RIG-I signaling, upregulated after dsRNA transfection or RNA virus infection in A549 cells (Cell Signal 2025); UniProt Q8IWZ4 curates 'induced upon RIG-I/DDX58 stimulation'. A separate paper (PMID 29186683) shows it degrades PRMT1 to promote ASK1 activation and cell death under oxidative stress, but in cancer cells and a xenograft with forced expression, not normal tissue.
best_source: PMID 40609779 (Wu et al., Cell Signal 2025, doi 10.1016/j.cellsig.2025.111973); UniProt Q8IWZ4; PMID 29186683
verify_reason: Both sources exist and say what is claimed, but neither is normal tissue. PMID 40609779 (Wu et al., Cell Signal 2025;134:111973) is an siRNA screen of 616 E3 ligases in A549 cells; the abstract says 'TRIM48 acts as an induced feedback regulator upon infection' and names it a negative feedback regulator of RIG-I, with overexpression and deficiency experiments. UniProt Q8IWZ4 curates 'induced upon RIG-I/DDX58 stimulation'. PMID 29186683 (Hirata et al., Cell Rep 2017) shows TRIM48 degrades PRMT1 to promote oxidative-stress ASK1 activation, using knockdown and forced expression in a cancer xenograft. All evidence is from tumor cell lines; I only read the abstract of the 2025 paper, so the magnitude of induction and absolute expression level are unchecked. Induction in normal infected human epithelium or immune cells is untested, so this stays a hypothesis, not a documented normal-tissue function. The assays are directed at TRIM48, though it sits in the chr11 TRIM48/TRIM49/TRIM51/TRIM64 cluster of similar genes and cross-reactivity of the siRNAs or primers was not verified.
criteria_gap: Induction by innate antiviral signaling is not captured by steady-state bulk, single-cell or IHC data (off-target TPM 0.2). Evidence is a single tumor cell line, so whether normal infected epithelium or immune cells induce it is untested; hence 'possible'.

claim: Human: UniProt (citing the chromosome 20 WAP-locus RT-PCR study) annotates WFDC8 as expressed ubiquitously, highest in epididymis, then testis and trachea. The abstract states this pattern for 'most' genes in the locus, which also includes WFDC9, WFDC10A and WFDC13, and notes some have high transcript levels in neural tissues; a proposed role is mucosal host defence.
verify_reason: PMID 12206714 exists, but its abstract describes the 14-gene locus collectively: 'several of the genes appear to be expressed ubiquitously, but, in most cases, the highest transcript levels are found in epididymis followed by testis and trachea', and 'some' genes are high in neural tissues. It does not name WFDC8 for trachea or neural expression. UniProt Q8IUA0 does carry the per-gene annotation 'expressed ubiquitously, highest in epididymis followed by testis and trachea', but it appears to restate the locus-level sentence. I could not retrieve the full text (PMC1222987) to check the WFDC8-specific data. This is one 2002 RT-PCR survey with no protein evidence and no cell type; the host-defence role is speculative in the source.
criteria_gap: Trachea and airway surface epithelium are probably not in the bulk tissue panels, and the existing verdict (specialized_tissue_expression, eye) does not cover airway. The evidence is one 2002 RT-PCR survey and the per-gene detail is in the full text, which was not opened.

claim: Mouse: Goofy is a Golgi membrane protein expressed specifically in olfactory and vomeronasal sensory neurons; knockout mice have mislocalised adenylyl cyclase III, shortened olfactory cilia and a raised odour detection threshold. No human olfactory expression data were located (search budget ran out).
verify_reason: Abstract of PMID 23926254 read and it matches the claim: Goofy is an integral membrane Golgi protein specific to mouse olfactory and vomeronasal sensory neurons; knockouts show impaired adenylyl cyclase III trafficking, stunted olfactory cilia and a higher odour threshold. Mouse only; no human olfactory expression data. Humans lack a functional vomeronasal organ, so only the olfactory epithelium part could carry over.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is absent from the bulk panels and the rare-cell screen. The catalog already carries a specialized_tissue_expression verdict for this gene; this adds the knockout phenotype.

gene: OR family, all 25 labels in this batch (family-level, not gene-specific)
claim: Human: all 25 proteins are annotated odorant receptors (UniProt), and a qPCR profile of whole human olfactory mucosa from 26 individuals detected 273 of 355 OR genes (77%). None of this batch's genes is named in the article text; per-gene values are only in its heatmap and supplementary tables, which I could not read.
best_source: DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0096333 (PMID 24800820, PMC4011832); per-gene confirmation would need its Figure 6 and supplementary tables
verify_reason: The source exists and supports the family-level statement: Verbeurgt et al. 2014 (PMID 24800820, PMC4011832) profiled 356 OR loci by TaqMan low-density array in whole olfactory mucosa collected post-mortem from 26 adults aged 39-81, and reports 273 (77%) OR genes above the cut-off of 5 copies/20 ng RNA, 90 of them in all 26 individuals. It is human, adult and non-reproductive tissue. But it is not evidence for any specific gene in this batch: a text search of the Europe PMC full-text XML found no mention of OR5V1, OR5K2, OR7E24 or OR6F1 (the only four batch genes named in the task; the other 21 labels were not given to me and were not checked). Per-gene values sit only in the figures and supplementary tables, which I did not read. About 23% of the assayed ORs were not detected, and the array covered 356 loci, so a given batch gene may be undetected or unassayed. The assay is per-gene TaqMan qPCR on bulk mucosa, with no cell-type resolution, so the 'olfactory sensory neuron' attribution is inferred. This stands as a panel-coverage gap (olfactory epithelium is unmeasured by the screen), not as a per-gene finding.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is absent from the HPA/GTEx bulk panels and from the rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut), so the expected normal adult expression site for every OR in the catalog is unmeasured. Coverage caveat: the session's shared web-search budget ran out after one search, so the 21 labels in not_researchable had no gene-specific literature search; they were checked only against UniProt (function 'Odorant receptor', no tissue, disease or induction annotation) and the text of Flegel 2013 (DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0055368), Verbeurgt 2014 and Massberg & Hatt 2018 (DOI 10.1152/physrev.00013.2017), none of which mention them. For the others, nothing new beyond the CSV: Flegel 2013 calls OR6F1 testis-specific, lists OR7E24 as the only intact OR7E member, and treats OR5K2's apparent expression as a likely artifact of a highly expressed surrounding gene region; the 2018 review only lists OR5K2, OR7E24 and OR6F1 among the 40 most expressed ectopic ORs, without a function.

claim: Family-level only: OR10A3 is an olfactory receptor gene, and human olfactory mucosa expresses a large part of the OR repertoire (PLoS One 2014, 'Profiling of olfactory receptor gene expression in whole human olfactory mucosa'). Gene-specific values were not checked.
best_source: PMID 24800820 (PMC4011832); gene-level data would be in its supplementary tables, not checked
verify_reason: The paper exists (Verbeurgt et al., PLoS One 2014): TaqMan array for 356 predicted OR loci in whole olfactory mucosa from 26 adults aged 39-81; on average 273 ORs detected, 90 in all 26 individuals. But OR10A3 does not appear anywhere in the PMC full text (only OR10A6 from that subfamily is named, in the deorphanized-receptor table). Per-gene results are in supplementary data that was not checked, so whether OR10A3 was on the array or detected is unknown. This stays a family-level inference, as the finding itself admits.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is not in the bulk panels or the rare-cell screen, so the expected physiological site of an OR gene is unsampled. The category is 'Cancer Antigen only' with no reproductive expression.

claim: Family-level only: OR10A7 is an olfactory receptor gene whose expected site is human olfactory mucosa, profiled for OR expression in PLoS One 2014. Gene-specific values were not checked.
verify_reason: Same source as OR10A3: the paper is real, human, adult olfactory mucosa, but OR10A7 is not mentioned in the PMC full text. Whether it was among the 356 loci probed or the roughly 273 detected was not verified (supplementary data not checked). Family-level inference only.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is not sampled by any part of the screen; a 0.0 off-target TPM only reflects the tissues that were profiled.

claim: Family-level only: OR10AG1 is an olfactory receptor gene whose expected site is human olfactory mucosa, profiled for OR expression in PLoS One 2014. Gene-specific values were not checked.
verify_reason: Same source: the paper is real, human, adult olfactory mucosa, but OR10AG1 is not mentioned in the PMC full text, and its presence on the 356-locus array or among detected genes was not verified. Family-level inference only.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is not sampled by any part of the screen.

claim: Family-level only: OR10D3 is an olfactory receptor gene whose expected site is human olfactory mucosa, profiled for OR expression in PLoS One 2014. Gene-specific values were not checked.
verify_reason: Same source: the paper is real, human, adult olfactory mucosa, but OR10D3 is not mentioned in the PMC full text, and its presence on the 356-locus array or among detected genes was not verified. The paper's abstract also notes that more than half of human OR loci are annotated nonfunctional, so membership in the family does not establish expression. Family-level inference only.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is not sampled by any part of the screen.

tissue: olfactory mucosa (applies to every olfactory receptor in this batch)
claim: Human: a TaqMan array covering 356 OR loci on whole olfactory mucosa from 26 adults (aged 39-81) detected on average 273 OR genes (about 77%) per person, 90 of them in all donors. The abstract names no individual genes, so per-gene values for the 25 receptors in this batch were not confirmed.
best_source: PMID 24800820 (Verbeurgt et al. 2014, PLoS One; PMC4011832), supplementary Table S1 for per-gene values
verify_reason: Source exists and the class-level statement is accurate: TaqMan array of 356 OR loci on post-mortem whole olfactory mucosa from 26 adults (39-81 y), mean 273 ORs detected, 90 in all donors. But OR13G1 is not named in the main text or Table 2 (per-gene data are only in supplementary tables S1/S3/S4 and a heatmap, which I could not read), so expression of OR13G1 specifically, and whether it was even among the 356 loci on the array, is unverified. The class-level gap (olfactory epithelium untested by the screen) is valid as a general caveat, not as a gene-specific finding. Tissue was cadaveric (27 h post-mortem; donors died of sepsis, haemorrhage, infarction), reasonably normal for nasal mucosa.
criteria_gap: Class-level gap filed under one gene: olfactory epithelium is a normal adult non-reproductive tissue absent from HPA/GTEx bulk, HPA single-cell and the rare-cell screen, so all 25 labels pass without their canonical tissue being tested. Each OR is expressed in a small fraction of olfactory neurons.

claim: Human nasal epithelial cells: OR2B3 was proposed by in silico docking as a receptor for linalyl acetate, and RT-PCR confirmed significant OR2B3 upregulation after exposure.
best_source: PMID 42066673 (Ferdousi et al. 2026, Biomed Pharmacother; doi 10.1016/j.biopha.2026.119446)
verify_reason: Source exists and abstract matches: OR2B3 proposed by in silico docking for linalyl acetate; RT-PCR confirmed upregulation of OR2B3 and OR6A2 in human nasal epithelial cells after treatment. This is a cultured cell model (donor/cell-line origin not given in abstract), odorant-induced, RNA only, no protein, no sequencing or paralog control stated (OR2B2/OR2B6 are close family members), and the receptor-ligand link is computational only. Nasal/olfactory epithelium is also the expected canonical site for an olfactory receptor, so it adds little as an off-target safety finding beyond the class-level gap. Abstract only; no open full text found.
criteria_gap: Nasal and olfactory epithelium are not in the bulk or rare-cell panels, and the CSV shows 0.0 TPM everywhere. Odorant-induced expression in cultured cells, abstract only, donor source not stated.

cell_type: olfactory sensory neuron (inferred from odorant-receptor function; cell type not stated in the record)
claim: Human: UniProt (O76001) curates OR2J3 as a functional odorant receptor for cis-3-hexen-1-ol, citing PubMed 22714804. Human variants Ala-113 and Gln-226 reduce the ability to smell the compound and the combined haplotype abolishes the receptor response, a benign specific anosmia rather than a disease.
best_source: McRae JF et al. Chem Senses 2012;37(7):585-93, PMID 22714804, PMCID PMC3408771, doi:10.1093/chemse/bjs049 (abstract opened; full text not read). UniProt O76001 is the curated summary of it.
verify_reason: The source exists and says what is claimed. UniProt O76001 (reviewed) curates OR2J3 as the odorant receptor for cis-3-hexen-1-ol and records that variants Ala-113 and Gln-226 reduce the ability to smell it, with the combined haplotype abolishing the response, all citing PMID 22714804. I opened the PubMed abstract (McRae et al., Chem Senses 2012;37:585-93): it is human, about OR2J3 specifically (coding regions of all 25 receptors in the chr6 cluster sequenced in 52 people; 13 receptors tested in vitro; all 5 OR2J3 haplotypes tested), and the T113A+R226Q haplotype explains 26.4% of variation in detection threshold. Weakened rather than confirmed for three reasons. (1) Neither source measures OR2J3 RNA or protein in olfactory epithelium or any tissue; the tissue and cell type are inferred from odorant-receptor function, as the finding itself admits, and the UniProt record has no tissue-specificity annotation. (2) The evidence is a genotype-to-detection-threshold association plus a heterologous cell assay, not a loss-of-function disease; the phenotype is a benign partial specific anosmia, and two other receptors in the region also respond to the compound, so OR2J3 is not the sole receptor. (3) It is not a vital-tissue function. The finding does stand as gene-specific human evidence that OR2J3 is a working olfactory receptor, in a tissue the screen does not sample.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is absent from the HPA/GTEx bulk panels, the HPA single-cell clusters and the rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut), so a working receptor in olfactory neurons is invisible to every part of the screen. The same blind spot applies in principle to all 25 odorant receptors in this batch, but only OR2J3 has gene-specific evidence in UniProt. COVERAGE CAVEAT FOR THIS BATCH: the session's web search budget was exhausted, so no literature search ran. All 25 labels were checked only against their reviewed UniProt records (function, tissue specificity, disease, induction, polymorphism, citation list). The primary paper (PMID 22714804) was not opened; the claim rests on UniProt's curated summary. Published ectopic-expression reports for these receptors, including OR2H1 and OR2J3, were not searched and would need a rerun.

claim: Human: OR52D1 was shown by calcium imaging against 100 odorants to be a functional odorant receptor with a narrow ligand repertoire. This supports a physiological role as an odorant receptor, presumably in olfactory sensory neurons, but the abstract reports no tissue expression data.
verify_reason: The source exists and its abstract says exactly what is claimed: human OR52D1 is a functional odorant receptor with a narrow repertoire in a calcium-imaging screen of 100 odorants (Sanz et al. 2005). The assay is gene-specific, but it is a receptor-function screen with no tissue data: nothing in the abstract shows OR52D1 expression in human olfactory epithelium or any other normal adult tissue. Expression in olfactory sensory neurons is an inference from the gene class. The general point stands that olfactory epithelium is unmeasured by the screen, but this paper is not direct evidence of normal-tissue expression. I did not look for a human olfactory mucosa RNA-seq dataset that would test it directly.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is absent from the HPA/GTEx bulk panels and from the rare-cell screen tissues, so the expected normal site of expression for every receptor in this batch is unmeasured. This applies as a class to all 25 OR genes here; OR52D1 is the only one with a gene-specific functional demonstration found.

claim: Mouse: Rtp1/Rtp2 double-knockout mice show olfactory receptor trafficking defects, fewer mature olfactory sensory neurons and reduced olfactory capacity (Sharma et al., eLife 2017). UniProt gives the human protein the same function (promotes cell-surface expression of olfactory receptors).
source: DOI 10.7554/eLife.21895 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/21895); known only from search-result summary, the article page would not load
best_source: PMID 28262096 / PMC5362263 (DOI 10.7554/eLife.21895); UniProt Q5QGT7 function is ECO:0000250 (by similarity)
verify_reason: Source exists and says what is claimed (Sharma et al., eLife 2017, PMID 28262096, full text read via PMC5362263): Rtp1/Rtp2 double-knockout mice have olfactory receptor trafficking defects, fewer mature olfactory sensory neurons and reduced olfactory capacity, with no gross defects outside the olfactory system. But it is mouse-only and a double knockout, so the phenotype cannot be assigned to Rtp2 rather than Rtp1. The UniProt human function line is by similarity (ECO:0000250), not human experimental data. No human olfactory epithelium expression data was opened.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is absent from the bulk RNA panels, the HPA single-cell clusters and the donor-level rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut).

claim: The secretoglobin family review (Jackson et al., Hum Genomics 2011) states SCGB1C1 is localised to Bowman's glands of the olfactory mucosa and may act as an odorant-binding protein. The primary localisation appears to rest on rat Ryd5 work, so human evidence is indirect.
best_source: PMID 1915264 (rat primary, abstract title only); PMID 22155607 / PMC3251818 (review)
verify_reason: The review (PMC3251818) does say SCGB1C1 'has been shown to be localised to Bowman's glands in the olfactory mucosa' and is thought to act as an odorant-binding protein. The underlying localisation is rat: Lu et al. 2011 (PMC3063214) explicitly says RYD5 was 'detected in Bowman's glands of rat olfactory mucosa', and the primary paper is the 1991 EMBO J rat study (PMID 1915264). No human olfactory mucosa data found.
criteria_gap: Olfactory mucosa is absent from every expression source the screen uses.

claim: Human: UniProt annotates TAAR2 as an orphan olfactory receptor for trace amines signalling through G(s); it also records no expression in several brain regions or liver (PubMed:10684976). Olfactory-epithelium expression is inferred from the function annotation, not a human tissue assay I opened.
verify_reason: UniProt Q9P1P5 does carry the 'orphan olfactory receptor' function, but it is annotated by similarity to a mouse protein (ECO:0000250, Q5QD04), not from a human assay. The only human tissue line is a negative one (not expressed in listed brain regions or liver, PubMed:10684976). Olfactory expression in humans is an inference, as the finding itself admits.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is absent from the bulk panels and rare-cell screen.

claim: Human: UniProt annotates TAAR9 as an olfactory receptor for trace amines (N,N-dimethylcyclohexylamine, beta-phenylethylamine) signalling through GNAL in mature olfactory neurons. A 2016 review also states human TAAR9 is expressed in brain without giving an assay (PMID 27424325).
verify_reason: UniProt Q96RI9 function text matches, but the olfactory-neuron statements are by similarity to mouse; the only human experimental citation (PubMed:34600890) is a ligand-activation assay, and there is no tissue-specificity entry. PMID 27424325 is a review whose abstract asserts brain expression for a list of TAARs with no assay. No human tissue evidence found.
criteria_gap: Olfactory epithelium is absent from the bulk panels and rare-cell screen; no tissue-specificity entry is curated, so this rests on the function annotation.

claim: Mouse: Beclin 2 is required for ligand-induced lysosomal degradation of several GPCRs via GASP1. Heterozygous knockout mice have defective autophagy, increased brain cannabinoid 1 receptor, elevated food intake, obesity and insulin resistance; homozygotes have decreased embryonic viability.
verify_reason: The abstract of PMID 23954414 says exactly what is claimed: GASP1-dependent GPCR degradation, heterozygous knockouts with defective autophagy, raised brain CB1R, increased food intake, obesity and insulin resistance, and reduced embryonic viability in homozygotes. The knockout is gene-specific, but the phenotype is mouse-only and no human loss-of-function disease was found. Mouse RT-PCR in the same paper shows beclin 2 in brain, skeletal muscle, thymus, placenta and uterus. It becomes relevant mainly alongside the human brain western blot in the same paper.
criteria_gap: A haploinsufficient metabolic and brain phenotype implies a physiological adult non-reproductive function at expression levels below every RNA threshold in the screen. No literature review was done for this gene.

claim: Mouse: Bhlhb4 (BHLHE23) is expressed in rod bipolar cells; adult knockouts lose the rod bipolar population and the scotopic ERG b-wave, resembling human congenital stationary night blindness. UniProt Q8NDY6 annotates the human protein by similarity for rod bipolar maturation and pancreatic/neuronal cell types.
verify_reason: The abstract of PMID 15363390 matches the claim: Bhlhb4 is expressed in rod bipolar cells, and adult knockouts lose the rod bipolar population and the scotopic ERG b-wave, resembling CSNB. This is mouse-only. UniProt Q8NDY6 gives the human function only 'by similarity' (ECO:0000250) and has no human tissue-specificity annotation. The source describes the role as maturation during postnatal development, so it does not show adult human expression. No human expression source was opened here.
criteria_gap: Rod bipolar cells are a small fraction of retina, so bulk RNA is diluted (HPA bulk: not detected; HPA single-cell: cell type enriched). The gene is 'below_screen' in the rare-cell eye screen and is not in the literature-reviewed subset.

claim: Mouse/rat: BMP-15 is expressed in mouse pituitary tissue and the LbetaT2 gonadotrope line, and selectively stimulates FSH-beta transcription and FSH secretion from primary pituitary cells. No human pituitary data were found, and OMIM describes mouse Bmp15 as ovary-only.
verify_reason: The abstract of PMID 12446622 supports the claim: BMP-15 is expressed in the LbetaT2 gonadotrope line and mouse pituitary tissue, and selectively stimulates FSH-beta transcription and FSH secretion from primary pituitary cells. It is rodent-only, from a single 2002 report, and the authors frame it as a hypothesis about FSH regulation in the estrous cycle, which is a reproductive-axis function. No human pituitary evidence was found.
criteria_gap: Gonadotrophs are a minority pituitary population and pituitary is not in the rare-cell screen; human bulk RNA is 0.1 TPM. Rodent only, and arguably a reproductive-axis role.

cell_type: somatic cells generally; shown in NIH3T3 fibroblasts at the centrosome
claim: Mouse: nested RT-PCR with sequencing found Ccdc42 transcript in brain and in all adult tissues tested except kidney, and endogenous CCDC42 protein localised to the centrosome in NIH3T3 fibroblasts. The full-length isoform was testis-only, so somatic cells may express a different isoform; the knockout paper (Pasek 2016) reports brain plus developing sperm expression with no phenotype beyond male sterility.
verify_reason: Source opened (Tapia Contreras and Hoyer-Fender, Front Cell Dev Biol 2019). It is mouse only, with no human expression data. The claim is slightly overstated: the first RT-PCR (exons 5-7) gave strong testis and epididymis signal and only weak brain signal; the nested PCR (exons 6+7) gave a product in all tissues except kidney. Sequencing confirmed the testis and epididymis products, and the ovary and NIH3T3 products, but the brain and other somatic tissue products are not reported as sequenced. Nested PCR detects trace transcript and says nothing about level. Full-length isoform 203 was testis-only, and the authors could not verify the short isoforms (201 not amplified; the 202 primer amplified an unrelated sequence). Endogenous centrosome staining in NIH3T3 is by antibody in a cell line with a no-primary control only. I did not open Pasek 2016. I read the first 100,000 characters of the page.
criteria_gap: Low-level expression of a short somatic isoform at the centrosome would sit below the bulk TPM threshold (CSV top off-target is blood at 2.97 TPM) and is not resolved by gene-level quantification. Mouse-only evidence.

cell_type: rod and cone photoreceptors (connecting cilium / transition zone)
claim: Mouse: centrin 1 protein localises to the photoreceptor connecting cilium and is lost in Cetn1 knockout retina. The knockout has no retinal degeneration and its only overt phenotype is male infertility, so the retinal function looks redundant with other centrins.
source: PMC3711207 (Avasthi et al., J Cell Sci 2013)
verify_reason: Source exists: Avasthi et al., J Cell Sci 2013, PMID 23641067 / PMC3711207; abstract read. It says CETN1 is expressed in male germ cells and photoreceptors and resides in the photoreceptor transition zone and connecting cilium; Cetn1 knockout mice are viable with no retinal degeneration, normal phototransduction-component localisation and normal transducin translocation; the only phenotype is male infertility. Mouse only, and the retinal role is non-essential. The specific statement that centrin 1 staining is lost in knockout retina is not in the abstract and was not verified. No human retina evidence was found.
criteria_gap: The CSV shows 0 TPM off-target and below_screen in the rare-cell screen, so a protein confined to the photoreceptor cilium would not be seen in bulk retina RNA or at the cluster level; no literature verdict. Mouse only, read from search-result summaries.

claim: Mouse: Cib3 transcripts are highly expressed in extrastriolar vestibular hair cells; Cib3 knockout mainly affects those cells, and Cib2/Cib3 double knockout disrupts stereocilia maintenance in all vestibular hair cells with severe balance deficits. UniProt annotates human CIB3 as an auxiliary subunit of the hair-cell mechanotransduction channel (by similarity).
verify_reason: PubMed abstract of PMID 37001993 (Wang et al., J Neurosci 2023) read and matches the claim: Cib3 transcripts are high in the extrastriolar region of mouse vestibular maculae, Cib3 knockout mainly affects extrastriolar hair-cell stereocilia, and Cib2/Cib3 double knockout abolishes MET currents and causes severe balance deficits. Knockouts are gene-specific, but CIB3 is redundant with CIB2 for MET. All of it is mouse; the UniProt Q96Q77 function line for human CIB3 is 'by similarity' only. No human expression or human loss-of-function evidence was found.
criteria_gap: Inner ear is absent from the bulk panels and the rare-cell screen; the CSV's top off-target is blood (6.59 TPM) and there is no literature verdict. Evidence is mouse only.

cell_type: gonadotrophs (colocalises with LH-beta in secretory granules)
claim: Mouse only: Cres (Cst8) mRNA and protein are expressed in anterior pituitary gonadotrophs, where it colocalises with LH-beta and is regulated by GnRH and androgens; CRES inhibits prohormone convertase 2. A 1.6 kb Cres promoter drives reporter expression in pituitary as well as germ cells. No human pituitary data were found.
verify_reason: Both sources exist and say what is claimed, but are mouse only: PMID 16837735 shows Cres mRNA and protein in male mouse anterior pituitary gonadotropes (colocalises with LH-beta, inhibits PC2, regulated by GnRH and steroids); PMID 15713831 shows the 1.6 kb mouse Cres promoter drives reporter in testis and anterior pituitary. One correction to the claim: the 2006 abstract says GnRH and estradiol negatively regulate Cres mRNA, while androgens restore CRES protein. No human pituitary evidence was cited or found, and the catalog's human RNA is near zero, so this stays a mouse-only possibility.
criteria_gap: Gonadotrophs are a minority population of the anterior pituitary, so bulk pituitary RNA dilutes the signal, and pituitary is not among the organs in the donor-level rare-cell screen. The catalog's highest off-target value is 0.1 TPM (retina), so the mouse finding may not carry over to human.

claim: Human: by quantitative RT-PCR, brain was the only somatic tissue positive for CT47, at an estimated 0.09% of the testis transcript level (weak placental expression also seen). The assay does not distinguish family members, so this applies to the CT47A copies and probably CT47B1.
source: PMID 16382448 (Chen et al., Genes Chromosomes Cancer 2006, doi:10.1002/gcc.20298)
best_source: PMID 16382448 (Chen et al., Genes Chromosomes Cancer 2006, doi:10.1002/gcc.20298)
verify_reason: Source exists and the abstract states it verbatim: brain was the only positive somatic tissue, at an estimated 0.09% of the testis transcript level, with weak placental expression. Human normal tissue qRT-PCR (commercial RNA panel; adult status presumed, not verified from the abstract). Weakened because the assay is family-level (>98% identity among at least 13 copies, cannot assign to any one CT47A/B member), the magnitude is about 1/1000 of testis, brain region and cell type are unspecified, and there is no protein evidence. The claim as stated is accurate and already self-described as probably not disqualifying.
criteria_gap: Multi-copy family with over 98% identity, so short-read atlases can under-count it through multi-mapping (mapping_risk is True in the CSV). The gene-specific qRT-PCR confirms a real but very low brain signal; the brain region and cell type are not specified. Magnitude is tiny and probably not disqualifying.

claim: Human: in two of three families in Xiao et al. 2001, DSPP missense mutations segregated with dentinogenesis imperfecta plus progressive high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (DFNA39). Secondary sources (MedlinePlus) say DSPP is active in the inner ear, with transcripts detected in mouse inner ear, but a causal role in hearing is described as unresolved.
best_source: Xiao et al. 2001, Nat Genet 27:201-4, PMID 11175790
verify_reason: The source exists and says this: two of three families had DGI1 plus progressive high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (DFNA39) with DSPP missense mutations. But the only expression evidence is in mouse inner ear ('transcripts of DSPP ... are also detected in the inner ear of mice'), with no human cochlear expression data. The human link is co-segregation in two families from one study, with no demonstrated causal role. I did not open the MedlinePlus statement. A PubMed search for DSPP and inner ear or cochlea returned no later study showing human inner-ear expression.
criteria_gap: Inner ear (cochlea) is not in any bulk, single-cell or rare-cell panel used by the screen.

tissue: kidney, salivary gland (also cartilage, liver, brain and bone in mouse)
cell_type: ductal / tubular epithelium (proximal, distal and collecting tubules; salivary striated and interlobular ducts)
claim: Human and monkey: Ogbureke and colleagues report DSPP protein by immunohistochemistry in salivary gland ducts (Ogbureke and Fisher 2004) and in kidney tubules, where it co-localises with MMP20 (2016). Mouse: Prasad et al. 2011 detected DSPP by RT-PCR, in situ and IHC in salivary gland, cartilage, liver, kidney and brain, but not heart or spleen, at levels far below dentin.
source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3261624 (mouse survey); human/monkey kidey study indexed in search results as PMID 27666430
best_source: Ogbureke et al. 2016, J Histochem Cytochem 64:623-36, PMID 27666430 (PMC5037501); Ogbureke and Fisher 2004, J Dent Res 83:664-70, PMID 15329369; Prasad et al. 2011, PMC3261624 (mouse)
verify_reason: All three sources exist and broadly say what is claimed. Ogbureke and Fisher 2004 (PMID 15329369) report DSPP in human and mouse salivary glands, and Ogbureke et al. 2016 (PMID 27666430) report DSPP with MMP20 in human and monkey kidney tubules by IHC, proximity ligation and immunofluorescence. The human evidence is antibody-only, from one group, with no knockout or orthogonal RNA validation. The Human Protein Atlas lists DSPP RNA as 'Not detected' with IHC 'Pending normal tissue annotation', so there is no independent protein confirmation. Prasad et al. 2011 is mouse-only, and the claim misdescribes it: the methods were RT-PCR, real-time PCR, Western, IHC and a lacZ knock-in (not in situ), and the abstract compares levels to bone (higher in salivary gland, cartilage, liver and kidney), not to dentin. I read abstracts only for all three papers.
criteria_gap: Protein-level evidence despite near-zero RNA: bulk kidney and salivary gland are in the panels and read below threshold, so this is antibody-based evidence contradicting the RNA atlases. It comes largely from one group and may reflect antibody cross-reactivity; needs checking against HPA IHC for DSPP.

claim: Human cell lines only: shRNA knockdown of EBLN1 in human oligodendroglia cells reduced proliferation and induced apoptosis (He et al. 2016, Int J Mol Sci), and siRNA knockdown in HeLa impaired cell-cycle transit and increased DNA damage (Sci Rep 2016). Protein existence is still contested (UniProt transcript-level evidence only) and another study reports the locus is epigenetically repressed in most tissues.
best_source: He et al. 2016, Int J Mol Sci, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4848891
verify_reason: The source (He et al. 2016, PMC4848891) exists and reports that shRNA knockdown of EBLN1 (81% mRNA reduction) in human OL cells suppressed proliferation, caused G2/M arrest and roughly doubled apoptosis (5.8% vs 3.0%). But OL is a permanent line established from human fetal brain, not normal adult tissue. EBLN1 protein was not measured and there was no rescue experiment, so off-target shRNA effects are not excluded. I did not open the HeLa knockdown paper or the epigenetic-repression study mentioned in the claim. This is not evidence of a physiological role in adult brain.
criteria_gap: A functional claim in a somatic (glial) cell type that expression thresholds cannot evaluate; the CSV maximum is cerebellum at 1.8 TPM, below the screen. Evidence is from immortalised lines, so it is weak support for a normal-tissue role.

claim: Human: mature FAM237A (also called neurosecretory protein GL, NPGL) binds and activates human GPR83 at nanomolar concentrations in transfected HEK293T cells, and the authors describe it as a neuropeptide ligand of a brain-specific receptor. This is in vitro receptor pharmacology, not a measurement of FAM237A in human tissue, and the pairing is not yet officially accepted.
verify_reason: The source exists and says what the claim reports (Li et al., FEBS J 2023): mature human FAM237A binds and activates human GPR83 at nanomolar range in transfected HEK293T cells, and the abstract calls FAM237A a 'so far rarely studied neuropeptide' and GPR83 'brain-specific'. The ligand is recombinant FAM237A itself, so it is gene-specific and not the paralog FAM237B (NPGM). But it is in vitro receptor pharmacology only: nothing in it measures FAM237A RNA or protein in any human tissue, adult or otherwise, and the abstract says the pairing had not been reproduced by other laboratories and GPR83 is still officially an orphan. It supports a plausible neuropeptide role, not demonstrated expression in normal adult human hypothalamus.
criteria_gap: A secreted neuropeptide made by a small hypothalamic neuron population would be diluted in bulk brain RNA (catalog shows 2.3 TPM in basal ganglia); the rare-cell screen marked it below_screen and it has no literature verdict.

claim: Mouse: NPGL (the Fam237a product) is described as a small secretory protein identified in the hypothalamus of birds and mammals; transgenic overexpression of Npgl in ICR mice increased white adipose tissue mass. Evidence is gain-of-function in rodents only; no loss-of-function model was found.
best_source: PMID 35742932 (Narimatsu Y et al., Int J Mol Sci 2022;23:6488, PMC9223635)
verify_reason: The source exists and matches the claim (Narimatsu et al., Int J Mol Sci 2022): NPGL is 'a small secretory protein identified in the hypothalamus of birds and mammals', and Npgl-transgenic ICR mice had increased white adipose tissue mass. The evidence is mouse-only and gain-of-function by transgenic overexpression, so it does not show an endogenous requirement or any human expression. The abstract contains no human data and no loss-of-function model. The transgene is Npgl specifically, so it is not paralog-ambiguous.
criteria_gap: Mouse-only functional evidence for an adult physiological role (energy balance) in a non-reproductive tissue; the screen has no functional or orthologue input and hypothalamic nuclei are poorly resolved in bulk panels.

claim: Human: the 1998 paper that first cloned FKBP6 states it is expressed in testis, heart, skeletal muscle, liver and kidney, and proposes that hemizygous deletion may contribute to hypercalcemia and growth delay in Williams syndrome. Only the abstract was read, the assay is not stated there, and later databases describe the gene as testis-restricted, so this may reflect low-specificity early methods.
best_source: PMID 9782077 (Meng X et al., Genomics 1998;52:130-7) for the claim; PMID 12764197 (Crackower et al., Science 2003;300:1291-5) as the gene-specific knockout counter-evidence
verify_reason: The source exists and the abstract says verbatim 'FKBP6 is expressed in testis, heart, skeletal muscle, liver, and kidney' and that hemizygous deletion 'may contribute to certain defects such as hypercalcemia and growth delay in WS' (Meng et al., Genomics 1998). It is about human FKBP6. The abstract does not state the assay, relative levels, or whether the tissues were adult; I did not read the full text. A 1998 cloning paper most likely used hybridisation or RT-PCR, which could cross-detect other FKBP family members, so I marked gene-specificity as unestablished and adult-normal as presumed. The Williams syndrome link is speculation in the abstract, not a demonstrated somatic function. Later gene-specific loss-of-function evidence points to a germline role: Fkbp6 knockout mice and as/as mutant rats have male sterility from a meiotic defect, females are fertile, and that abstract reports no somatic phenotype (Crackower et al., Science 2003). This is an unreplicated early report that conflicts with the modern atlases, not evidence of a somatic function.
criteria_gap: Gene-specific report of somatic expression that the RNA atlases do not show (catalog max 2.87 TPM in blood, 0.4 nTPM); the existing literature verdict covers only the lung multiciliated-cell rare-cell hit, not this heart/muscle/liver/kidney claim. The label is also flagged as a mapping risk.

claim: Mouse: Foxr1 knockout gives about 23.5% survival to postnatal day 21, lower body weight, a thinner cortical plate and enlarged ventricles; mouse qPCR detected Foxr1 mRNA in heart, liver and lung as well as brain. Human: one proband with a de novo M280L variant had postnatal microcephaly and progressive brain atrophy (confounded by a co-occurring ATP1A3 variant), and the paper cites Human Brain Transcriptome data that brain expression is maintained throughout life.
verify_reason: The source exists and the stated numbers check out (Mota et al., PLoS Genet 2021, first 100k characters read): about 23.5% of Foxr1 knockout mice survive to P21, they weigh 24.5% less, the cortical plate is about 11.3% thinner and ventricles are 34.6% larger. Mouse qPCR detected Foxr1 mRNA in heart, liver and lung, with higher expression in brain at embryonic day 17. The human proband has a de novo M280L variant with postnatal microcephaly and progressive brain atrophy, and the ATP1A3 variant was returned to the family as a partial diagnosis. The paper cites Human Brain Transcriptome data that brain expression 'is maintained throughout life'. As a normal-adult-human finding it is weak: the knockout phenotype is mouse and developmental, the highlighted brain qPCR signal is embryonic, the single human case is confounded, and the only adult human evidence is a secondary citation of an array atlas at low level, not a gene-specific assay in adult tissue. The paper itself says FOXR1 is expressed at low levels in most tissues and mainly in brain and reproductive organs.
criteria_gap: The knockout phenotype is largely developmental (expected), but the cited lifelong low-level brain expression and the low-level multi-tissue qPCR signal sit under the bulk TPM threshold (catalog max 1.26 TPM in blood); the gene has no literature verdict and was below the rare-cell screen.

tissue: liver, colon (also trace T cells and brain per UniProt-derived annotation)
claim: Human: RT-PCR and RACE in normal tissues found FUT5 expressed at lower levels and in fewer cell types than FUT3 and FUT6 (PMID 7650030, abstract read). UniProt-derived annotation and NCBI Gene (seen in search results only) list liver, colon and oesophagus, with colon at about 6 RPKM in the HPA RNA-seq set.
verify_reason: Abstract of PMID 7650030 read: it studies FUT3, FUT5 and FUT6 in normal human tissues by RT-PCR, RACE and Northern and says only that 'FUT5 expression was lower and restricted to fewer cell types'. It names kidney, liver and colon for FUT3 and FUT6 transcripts, not for FUT5. The liver and colon attribution comes from UniProt Q11128, which I confirmed reads 'Liver, colon and testis and trace amounts in T-cells and brain'; it carries no evidence code. The NCBI Gene figure of about 6 RPKM in colon was not checked and would be subject to the same FUT3/FUT6 multi-mapping the claim raises. Whether the 1995 primers separated FUT5 from its near-identical neighbours cannot be judged from the abstract. Low-level normal expression in a few cell types is supported; the specific tissues are not.
criteria_gap: FUT5 is near-identical to FUT3 and FUT6 (the catalog flags mapping risk), so multi-mapped reads may be assigned away from it and the 0.81 TPM maximum may understate gut and liver expression; gene-specific PCR detects it in normal tissue.

tissue: hypothalamus (arcuate nucleus, median eminence) and posterior pituitary
cell_type: arcuate neurons; pituicytes of the neurohypophysis
claim: In adult macaque, GALP mRNA is confined to the arcuate nucleus, median eminence and neurohypophysis (PMID 11861493); in rat it is in arcuate neurons and pituicytes (PMID 14962070) and is induced by leptin, so expression is state-dependent. No human-specific expression paper was found in this session.
verify_reason: Both abstracts were read and say what the claim reports: in situ hybridisation confines GALP mRNA to arcuate nucleus, median eminence and neurohypophysis in macaque (PMID 11861493), and to arcuate neurons and pituicytes in rat (PMID 14962070). The evidence is macaque and rat only; no human expression data. The state-dependence in the rat paper is thyroid hormone and lactation (lactation raises neurohypophysis GALP), not leptin; leptin regulation is only cited as background in the macaque abstract. In situ probes are gene-specific, and the pattern is conserved across primate and rodent, so human arcuate expression is plausible but unshown.
criteria_gap: Bulk hypothalamus and pituitary RNA dilutes a small arcuate/pituicyte population (catalog max is 0.6 TPM in cortex), and the rare-cell screen's brain data are unlikely to sample arcuate nucleus or neurohypophysis. Expression also varies with metabolic state (leptin, fasting, osmotic stimuli in rodents).

claim: Mouse: MGI states that Galr3-null mice show increased anxiety-like behaviour and abnormal social investigation, and a separate report describes an alcohol-preferring phenotype; a 2023 review abstract describes GALR3 as broadly expressed in the nervous system including the retina and as a modulator of immune and inflammatory responses (a murine colitis study, PMID 33436730, was listed but its abstract was not read).
verify_reason: PMID 36693600 abstract read: it states GALR3 is 'broadly expressed in the nervous system, including the retina' and modulates immune and inflammatory responses. It is a primary mouse study, not a review, and the functional data are mouse disease models (light damage, P23H Rho), where GALR3 loss or the antagonist SNAP-37889 was protective, plus ARPE19 cells. The MGI behavioural phenotypes and the alcohol-preference report were not opened and remain unverified. All mouse; no human normal-tissue expression or loss-of-function evidence. The knockout is gene-specific, but SNAP-37889 selectivity was not assessed here.
criteria_gap: A functional receptor acting at very low transcript abundance in neurons is not caught by TPM thresholds; knockout phenotypes are not part of the screen. Mouse only, and GALR3 antibodies are reported as poorly validated.

claim: Mouse: connexin 23 (Gje1) is expressed in lens fibre cells and the Aey12 point mutant arrests lens development with small eyes, although a targeted null has transparent lenses. For human, the search results state that the ortholog carries a stop mutation at the start of exon 3 and that no Cx23 mRNA was found in human eye, so this is likely not a human liability.
source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2719720 and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4920263 (seen in search results, not opened)
verify_reason: PMC2719720 opened (Sonntag et al., 'Mouse lens connexin23 (Gje1) does not form functional gap junction channels but causes enhanced ATP release from HeLa cells'). It confirms the mouse part (Cx23 in newly formed lens fibre cells) and the human part: a stop mutation at the start of exon 3, 'No Cx23 mRNA was found in human eye', no transcript by RT-PCR or Northern in human lens and retina, and the conclusion that Cx23 is a pseudogene in primates.
