The statement is accurate as written, but as a human normal-tissue liability it is negative: the only human evidence argues against lens expression. PMC4920263 (Aey12 mutant and null) was not opened.
criteria_gap: Lens is absent from all panels. Reported mainly so the lens is ruled out explicitly: the human evidence points to no lens expression and questions whether the human protein is made at all.

claim: Mouse: Gsc2 (Goosecoid-like, Gscl) expression in adult brain is restricted to the interpeduncular nucleus. Knockout mice have reduced REM sleep, fewer REM episodes, lower REM theta power and lose Dgcr14 expression in that nucleus, with apparently normal anatomy (Funato et al., PNAS 2010). Mouse only; the gene lies in the human 22q11 deletion region.
best_source: PMID 20921407; doi:10.1073/pnas.1012764107 (abstract read via PubMed E-utilities)
verify_reason: Source exists and its abstract matches the claim: Funato et al., PNAS 2010 (PMID 20921407) states that Gscl expression is restricted to the interpeduncular nucleus, and that Gscl-/- mice have apparently normal IP anatomy and connections but reduced total REM sleep time, fewer REM episodes, reduced REM theta power, increased arousability during REM, and loss of Dgcr14 expression in the IP. Gscl is the mouse ortholog of human GSC2 (not GSC), and the knockout is gene-specific. Weakened because it is mouse only: no human adult expression or protein data are given, and the phenotype is a mild sleep-architecture change, not a vital-tissue defect. Only the abstract was read (PMC full text blocked by captcha).
criteria_gap: The interpeduncular nucleus is a tiny midbrain nucleus not sampled as its own subregion; the 2.4 TPM pons / 2.5 nTPM value is probably its diluted signal and sits below the screen. The single-cell rare-cell brain panel is unlikely to include this nucleus.

tissue: brain (adult subventricular zone neural stem cell niche)
claim: Mouse: Gsx2 is expressed in a regionally restricted subset of adult SVZ neural stem cells in the intact brain, where it promotes their activation and lineage progression. After hypoxia-ischemia or neurotoxic injury it is induced across wide areas of the niche and is required for injury-induced neurogenesis (Lopez-Juarez et al., Genes Dev 2013). Mouse only; not shown in adult human.
best_source: PMID 23723414; doi:10.1101/gad.217539.113 (abstract read via PubMed E-utilities)
verify_reason: Source exists and its abstract says what is claimed: Lopez-Juarez et al., Genes Dev 2013 (PMID 23723414) reports that in the intact adult mouse brain Gsx2 is expressed in a regionally restricted subset of SVZ neural stem cells, promotes their activation and lineage progression, is ectopically induced in damaged brains outside its normal domain, and is required for injury-induced SVZ neurogenesis. It is about Gsx2 itself (not Gsx1) and uses mouse genetics, so it is gene-specific. Weakened because it is mouse only, with no adult human data, and adult human SVZ neurogenesis is far more limited than in mouse, so transfer is uncertain. The specific injury models (hypoxia-ischemia, neurotoxic lesion) were not checked: PMC full text was blocked by a captcha and the abstract only says 'damaged brains'.
criteria_gap: Bulk brain-subregion RNA dilutes a rare periventricular stem-cell population (basal ganglia 1.9 TPM may be its trace). The rare-cell screen flagged only an eye RPE signal, which was dismissed. Injury-induced expression is invisible to any steady-state atlas.

claim: Mouse: the ortholog H2A.B.3 is most highly expressed in testis, followed by brain. In brain chromatin it is found at transcription start sites of active genes and replaces H2A.Z at intron-exon boundaries, correlating with expression and exon inclusion (Soboleva et al., PLoS Genet 2017). Mouse only; the knockout phenotype reported so far is male subfertility, with no brain phenotyping found.
source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5345878 (PLoS Genet 2017, H2A.B in testis and brain RNA processing)
best_source: PMID 28234895; doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1006633 (abstract via PubMed, full text via Europe PMC PMC5345878)
verify_reason: Source exists (Soboleva et al., PLoS Genet 2017, PMID 28234895, doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1006633) and supports the claim. Abstract: H2A.B 'is most highly expressed in the testis followed by the brain in mammals'; H2A.B.3 replaces H2A.Z at intron-exon boundaries in testis and brain, correlating with expression and exon inclusion. Full text: H2A.B.3 ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR in mouse hippocampus show it at the TSS and gene body of active genes, and S3 Fig shows immunostaining in hippocampal neurons. The introduction is more modest than the abstract: 'highly expressed in the adult testis with some expression in the brain'. Weakened because all data are mouse H2A.B.3, with no human tissue. It is also not gene-specific for human H2AB1: mouse H2A.B.3 is one of three mouse H2A.B genes and has no one-to-one mapping to human H2AB1 versus H2AB2/H2AB3, which encode near-identical proteins that an antibody or ChIP cannot separate. The 'no brain phenotyping in the knockout' statement was not checked.
criteria_gap: Human brain RNA is low (0.7 TPM white matter) and below the screen, and the label carries mapping risk across the near-identical H2AB1/2/3 copies. Chromatin-level protein evidence in brain is not captured by RNA thresholds or HPA immunohistochemistry.

tissue: brain (hippocampus; also cerebellum and cerebral cortex by qPCR)
cell_type: subpopulation of NeuN-positive neurons outside the dentate gyrus
claim: In human tissue, H3.X/Y mRNA was detected by qPCR in cerebellum, cerebral cortex and hippocampus (not thalamus) as well as testis. Immunofluorescence with a monoclonal anti-H3.X/Y antibody stained a small subpopulation of hippocampal neurons. In human U2OS cells, starvation and high cell density increased the number of H3.Y-expressing cells.
source: PMID 20819935 (Wiedemann et al., J Cell Biol 2010; PMC2935562)
verify_reason: Wiedemann 2010 (PMC2935562) does report H3.X/Y mRNA by qPCR in human brain regions (all except thalamus) and testis, and immunofluorescence of NeuN-positive neurons outside the dentate gyrus in human hippocampus sections. But the monoclonal antibody was raised against a peptide shared by H3.X and H3.Y and the main amplicon is H3.X+Y, so the assay does not separate H3Y1 (H3.Y) from its paralog H3Y2 (H3.X); H3.X mRNA was also detected in brain. Donor age and health of the commercial frozen hippocampus sections are not stated, and the brain RNA set included fetal brain. The U2OS starvation/density result is in a tumor cell line; starvation alone had a minor effect.
criteria_gap: Protein in a sparse neuronal subpopulation gives near-zero bulk RNA (0.2 TPM cortex). The rare-cell status is 'below_screen', and stress-induced expression is not modelled. The gene is also flagged mapping_risk, so atlas quantification of this primate-specific histone is unreliable.

claim: In rat and mouse, HMGB4 (and the rat paralog HMGB4L1) transcripts are detected by RT-PCR/qPCR in cultured hippocampal, cerebellar and embryonic cortical neurons. An antibody that is not HMGB4-specific stains differentiated NeuN-positive neurons, and HMGB4 regulates neural differentiation genes. The authors note somatic expression is extremely low and adult brain evidence is indirect.
verify_reason: PMID 27608812 (PMC5036535) exists and reports RT-PCR bands for HMGB4 and HMGB4L1 in cultured rat hippocampal and cerebellar neurons and qPCR in mouse E14 cortical neurons. Evidence is rodent, mostly cultured or embryonic cells. The anti-HMGB4 and anti-HMGB4L1 antibodies cross-react, so the neuronal staining cannot separate HMGB4 from the rat paralog. The authors state most somatic cells do not express HMGB4 or do so at very low levels. No direct human tissue measurement of HMGB4: human data are HEK 293T and NTERA-2 lines.
criteria_gap: Consistent with the low hypothalamus signal (1.1 TPM) already in the catalog. It adds rodent gene-specific evidence that this is genuine neuronal expression rather than noise, but there is no human adult protein data and the gene is 'below_screen' in the rare-cell screen.

claim: Mouse: RT-PCR and western blot identified two short cytoplasmic Slo3 isoforms (C-terminal 381 amino acids) expressed in somatic tissues including brain, kidney and eye, while the full-length channel is testis-only. Any epitope from the C-terminal tail would therefore not be testis-restricted in mouse; human somatic isoforms were not examined.
verify_reason: PMID 31270758 abstract opened and matches the claim: two short Slo3 isoforms encoding the terminal 381 amino acids are expressed in mouse brain, kidney and eye by RT-PCR, with western blot corroboration in brain and testis only (not kidney or eye); full-length channel is testis-only. Mouse only, no functional role shown, and human somatic isoforms were not examined. UniProt A8MYU2 lists human KCNU1 as testis-specific. The link to the 0.8 TPM pons value is the finder's inference, not from the paper.
criteria_gap: Gene-level TPM hides isoform-specific somatic expression of a 3' fragment; the catalog's highest off-target value is in pons (0.8 TPM), consistent with a low-level brain transcript the threshold ignores. Mouse only.

claim: Human: a bioinformatic survey of GEO and HPA datasets reports LGALS16 detected by microarray in diverse human cells and tissues, with expression changes in brain diseases and diabetes (Kaminker 2021). This is atlas and microarray evidence with no gene-specific validation outside placenta.
verify_reason: Kaminker and Timoshenko 2021 (PMID 34944551) exists and its abstract says LGALS16 'is detected by microarrays in diverse human cells/tissues and alters expression in association with cancer, diabetes, and brain diseases'. This is a bioinformatic survey of GEO microarray and HPA data; the only wet-lab work is in placental cell lines (BeWo, JEG-3). Microarray probes cannot reliably separate LGALS16 from LGALS13/14, and much of the non-placental signal is from disease datasets and cell lines. It adds no gene-specific evidence beyond the atlases the screen already uses.
criteria_gap: Adds little beyond the catalog's 0.9 TPM in hypothalamus, but suggests the low brain signal is reproducible across datasets rather than noise. Microarray cross-hybridisation with LGALS13/14 is a plausible alternative explanation.

claim: Mouse: LRRC52 is the BK-channel gamma-2 subunit in cochlear inner hair cells. In Lrrc52 knockout mice, BK current activation shifts by more than +200 mV and BK channel localisation is disrupted (Lingle 2019); nested PCR, immunohistochemistry and proximity ligation independently show LRRC52 transcript and protein with BK-alpha at the hair cell neck (Lang 2019, PMID 31348683). No human inner-ear data found.
best_source: PMID 31451634 (Lingle 2019, PNAS); supporting PMID 31348683 (Lang 2019, FASEB J)
verify_reason: Both sources exist and say what is claimed: Lingle 2019 (PMID 31451634) shows the >+200 mV BK activation shift and disrupted BK localisation in Lrrc52 knockout inner hair cells (Lrrc26 knockout had no effect), and Lang 2019 (PMID 31348683) shows nested PCR, immunohistochemistry and proximity ligation. The assays are gene-specific, but all evidence is mouse; there is no human inner-ear expression or human hearing-loss data. Real function, mouse-only.
criteria_gap: Inner ear is absent from the HPA/GTEx bulk panels and from the rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut). Inner hair cells are a tiny non-regenerating population, so the catalog value (3.8 TPM, parathyroid) says nothing about this site. Coverage note for the whole batch: the session's web search budget was already exhausted, so every gene was researched through UniProt, PubMed and Europe PMC queries only; HPA, GeneCards, OMIM and MGI pages were not opened.

claim: Human: after fatal neurotoxicity with an anti-MAGE-A3/A9/A12 TCR, quantitative PCR, Nanostring and deep sequencing of human brain showed MAGE-A12 expression 'and possibly MAGE-A1, MAGE-A8, and MAGE-A9'; a pan-MAGE-A antibody stained rare neurons in normal brain (Morgan 2013). The MAGE-A1 signal is described only as possible.
best_source: PMID 23377668, full text PMC3581823 (Nanostring and Table 6 RNA-seq sections)
verify_reason: Morgan 2013 (PMID 23377668, full text PMC3581823) exists and the abstract wording matches ('MAGE-A12 was expressed in human brain (and possibly MAGE-A1, MAGE-A8, and MAGE-A9)'). The MAGE-A1 evidence is thin on inspection. The neuron staining used antibody 6C1, which the authors verified recognises MAGE-A1, A2, A3, A4, A6, A9, A10 and A12, so it is not gene-specific. The MAGE-A1 RNA signal comes from Nanostring on commercial normal brain RNA against 'an arbitrary cut-off value of 20' (negative-probe mean 8.7 +/- 8.6), described as 'may be present'. The RNA-seq of six control frontal cortices named only MAGE-A12 and MAGE-A8 as expressed, not MAGE-A1. So the one deep-sequencing assay did not support MAGE-A1 in brain; the toxicity is attributed to MAGE-A12.
criteria_gap: The catalog reports 0.0 TPM off-target. Expression confined to rare neurons falls below bulk brain RNA and may fall below the rare-cell screen threshold, yet it was enough to be clinically lethal for a sibling gene.

claim: Human: UniProt annotates MRGPRG as an orphan receptor that may regulate nociceptor function and pain sensation, by similarity to other MRGPR family members only. No gene-specific human DRG expression data were found in this session, so this is family-level inference.
source: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q86SM5 (UniProt Q86SM5, function field, by similarity)
best_source: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q86SM5 (function field, by similarity only). Not opened, suggested check: Flegel et al. 2015 PLoS ONE human trigeminal/DRG RNA-seq supplementary tables
verify_reason: UniProt Q86SM5 does say 'Orphan receptor. May regulate nociceptor function and/or development, including the sensation or modulation of pain (By similarity)', so the source exists and is quoted correctly. But the evidence code is ECO:0000250 (sequence similarity) with no cited publication and no tissue-specificity field: there is no human measurement, and nothing specific to MRGPRG rather than the MRGPR family. One web search found no human DRG expression data for MRGPRG. This is an untested hypothesis, not evidence of normal-tissue expression.
criteria_gap: If expressed like its paralogs it would sit in sensory ganglia, which no bulk panel or rare-cell tissue in the screen covers; worth a check against a human DRG RNA-seq dataset. Evidence here is annotation by similarity, not measurement.

claim: Oncomodulin (beta-parvalbumin; human copies OCM and OCM2) has a cochlear role in mouse: Europe PMC lists oncomodulin-deficient mouse studies reporting early progressive hearing loss and increased noise susceptibility in adults (eNeuro 2026; Int J Mol Sci 2026). This is mouse-only evidence taken from titles; the UniProt entries for human OCM2 (P0CE71) and OCM (P0CE72) carry no tissue annotation.
best_source: PMID 42161597 (PMC13238953) and PMID 42123419 (PMC13163798), both mouse Ocm knockout
verify_reason: Both cited papers exist and their abstracts support the mouse claim: PMID 42161597 (eNeuro 2026) reports Ocm-/- adult mice get permanent threshold shifts after moderate noise and early-onset hearing loss; PMID 42123419 (Int J Mol Sci 2026) calls OCM the most abundant Ca2+ buffer in mature outer hair cells and reports hearing decline in Ocm-KO mice. All of it is mouse Ocm. UniProt P0CE71 (human OCM2) has no function or tissue annotation and HPA 'Not detected'; P0CE72 (human OCM) has only a generic calmodulin-like function line and HPA 'Tissue enhanced (brain)'. Nothing distinguishes human OCM2 from OCM, and no human cochlear data was found in the cited sources. Human relevance is inference from the mouse ortholog.
criteria_gap: Inner ear is absent from every bulk panel and from the rare-cell screen. The label is flagged mapping_risk (OCM/OCM2 near-identical paralogs), so the RNA values are unreliable too.

tissue: brain (inferred from neuron-derived vesicles in serum and CSF)
claim: Human: the same traumatic brain injury study named OR14A2 among olfactory receptor mRNAs elevated in neuronally derived extracellular vesicles from serum and CSF.
source: PMID 38474024 (Bhomia et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci)
best_source: PMID 38474024 (Bhomia et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci; PMC10931597)
verify_reason: Abstract confirmed: OR14A2 named among OR mRNAs elevated in neuronal exosomes from serum/CSF of TBI patients. Same limits as OR1B1: patients with brain injury, vesicle RNA with inferred origin, authors point to olfactory neuroepithelium damage as a source, no tissue-level or protein evidence, and OR14A2 is a known multi-mapping risk. Abstract only (full text blocked). Not evidence of normal brain expression.
criteria_gap: Same gap as OR1B1: possible injury-induced neuronal expression not captured by constitutive bulk RNA. Weak, abstract-level, and the label is flagged mapping_risk.

tissue: brain (inferred from neuron-derived vesicles in serum and CSF)
claim: Human: RNA-seq of neuronally derived extracellular vesicles from serum and CSF of traumatic brain injury patients found OR1B1 and OR14A2 mRNAs among olfactory receptor transcripts at elevated concentrations, with serum validation in mild TBI.
source: PMID 38474024 (Bhomia et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci)
best_source: PMID 38474024 (Bhomia et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci; PMC10931597)
verify_reason: Abstract confirmed: OR1B1 named among OR mRNAs elevated in neuronal exosomes from serum and CSF of severe TBI patients, with serum validation in mild TBI. But this is injured patients, not normal tissue; RNA in circulating vesicles, with tissue of origin only inferred; the authors themselves attribute it partly to damaged olfactory neuroepithelium (the expected canonical OR tissue) rather than brain; no in situ or protein evidence in brain; low-count RNA-seq of OR family members is prone to multi-mapping. I could not open the full text (PMC blocked), abstract only. Does not demonstrate brain expression.
criteria_gap: Suggests injury-induced neuronal expression, which constitutive bulk brain RNA would miss. Weak: patients only, RNA only, abstract level. Both labels are also multi-mapping risks in this family (OR14A2 is flagged mapping_risk in the CSV).

claim: Human: OR4M1 and OR11H1 were detected in PBMC and down-regulated after traumatic brain injury; the abstract states these receptors are ectopically expressed in multiple brain regions (species and method not given) and that OR4M1 activation attenuated abnormal tau phosphorylation via JNK signalling (Zhao et al. 2013).
best_source: PMID 23241557 (Zhao et al., J Alzheimers Dis 2013; PMC3968322)
verify_reason: The source exists and the expression part is human and normal: full text (PMC3968322) shows OR4M1 mRNA in PBMC of healthy controls (microarray, then SYBR qPCR) and by RT-PCR in postmortem temporal, entorhinal and occipital cortex and hippocampus from 4 neurologically normal cases, so the species and method the claim left open are human RT-PCR. Weaker than claimed in two ways. (1) The tau/JNK result is not endogenous function: human OR4M1 was overexpressed by lentivirus in embryonic mouse cortico-hippocampal neurons and stimulated with acetophenone. (2) Expression rests on SYBR qPCR for a single-exon gene with a close paralog (OR4M2); I found no mention of DNase treatment, no-RT controls or amplicon sequencing, so genomic DNA carry-over and paralog cross-amplification are not excluded. Single lab, small cohorts, RNA only, no protein or cell-type localisation. Consistent with the catalog's very low blood signal rather than a missed function.
criteria_gap: Catalog shows 0.06 TPM in blood and no brain signal. A single-lab expression-profiling claim with functional follow-up; if real, the level is below the bulk and rare-cell thresholds.

claim: Human: OR52L1 is listed among olfactory receptors downregulated in frontal cortex area 8 of Parkinson disease patients versus controls in a transcriptomics study, which implies detectable expression in control adult human cortex. Only the abstract was read; the assay details and control expression level were not confirmed.
best_source: PMID 23656994 (abstract only; full text not checked)
verify_reason: The source exists and its abstract does list OR52L1 among olfactory receptors downregulated in frontal cortex area 8 in Parkinson disease (Garcia-Esparcia et al. 2013). But expression in normal cortex is only inferred from a disease-versus-control comparison; the abstract gives no control expression level for OR52L1. The cell-level evidence in the abstract (neuronal expression) concerns the downstream machinery (ADCY3, Golf, RTP1/2, REEP1, UGT1A6), not OR52L1. The abstract says only 'a transcriptomics approach'; I did not open the full text, so the platform and whether OR52L1 itself was validated by a gene-specific assay are unverified. Olfactory receptor paralogs are highly similar, so specificity cannot be assumed. The catalog's bulk brain RNA is near zero, so this is at most a hint of low-level transcript.
criteria_gap: Bulk brain RNA is near zero for this gene in the catalog (0.43 TPM max, in blood); a study using a targeted transcriptomic approach on cortex reports it as a regulated transcript. The rare-cell screen status is below_screen, so a low-level neuronal signal would not have been graded.

claim: Human: family-based whole-exome sequencing reported a missense variant in OR52L1 in affected individuals with retinitis pigmentosa, proposed as a candidate alongside OR56A5 and CTSD. This is a genetic association in a small family study with no expression or functional data in the abstract.
verify_reason: The source exists (Lin et al. 2021, PMC8198027) and reports an OR52L1 missense variant shared by all five affected members of one retinitis pigmentosa family. The full text states that SIFT, PolyPhen2, LRT and MetaSVM predicted the OR52L1 and OR56A5 variants to be benign and tolerated. So this is not a loss-of-function finding, and the paper's own annotation argues against causality. There is no retinal expression or functional data; the 'detecting visible light' link comes from an in silico protein-interaction network. A shared variant in a single family, with no segregation statistics or replication, is not evidence of a retinal function.
criteria_gap: The screen uses expression only; a candidate disease-gene link to a vital sensory tissue is not captured by RNA or IHC thresholds. Evidence is weak (candidate variant, not established causality).

claim: Mouse Otop1 is expressed in vestibular supporting cells and is required for otoconia formation; mutant and knockout mice have otoconial agenesis and vestibular dysfunction. UniProt extends the function to human by similarity only.
verify_reason: Mouse only, as the claim itself says. PMID 12651873 maps the tilted/mergulhador mutations to Otop1 and reports expression in the macula of the developing otocyst, so part of the evidence is developmental. PMID 20554841 shows OTOP1 at the apex of supporting cells using knockout mice and utricular organ culture. UniProt extends this to human by similarity; no human tissue or human disease evidence is cited.
criteria_gap: Inner ear is not in any bulk or single-cell panel used by the screen.

claim: OTUD6A is reported to rise in kidney tissue of nephropathy patients and angiotensin II-treated mice, located mainly in tubular epithelial cells; knockout mice are protected from angiotensin II kidney injury, cardiac hypertrophy and colitis. Knockouts are healthy at baseline, so the gene acts in disease-induced states rather than normal physiology.
verify_reason: Sources exist and match the claim. The human data are diseased tissue: nephropathy kidney (PMID 38105755) and hypertrophic heart (PMID 38342418). The rest is angiotensin II, aortic constriction and colitis models in mice, where knockouts are protected rather than harmed. No evidence of expression or function in healthy adult human tissue; detection is antibody-based and all three organ papers come from one Wenzhou group.
criteria_gap: Stress- and inflammation-induced expression in kidney, heart and macrophages is not captured by healthy-donor atlases. The studies come from a small group of related labs and rely on antibody detection.

claim: Adult P2Y4-null mice have microcardia; the receptor is expressed in cardiac endothelial cells, not cardiomyocytes, and the authors also detected P2Y4 in human cardiac microvessels. Loss of the receptor alters the response to cardiac ischemia in mice.
verify_reason: PMID 22437266 supports microcardia in adult P2Y4-null mice and expression in cardiac endothelial cells, not cardiomyocytes. The phenotype arises from reduced post-natal heart growth, so it is developmental, and PMID 25595790 shows the knockout is protected in infarction. The human part is one sentence in the abstract ('We also detected P2Y4 expression in human cardiac microvessels') with no method or tissue status given there.
criteria_gap: Expression confined to a minority endothelial population is diluted in bulk heart; the knockout phenotype is in a vital tissue although it is developmental and the adult consequence is mild.

tissue: gastrointestinal tract, endocrine glands, brain, spleen, pancreas
cell_type: not resolved (glandular epithelium, stroma and vascular endothelium shown only in decidua)
claim: Human: UniProt Q8TCW9 lists PROKR1 (prokineticin receptor 1, a Gq-coupled GPCR) as expressed in stomach, throughout the small intestine, colon, rectum, thyroid, pituitary, salivary gland, adrenal gland, brain, spleen, prostate and pancreas, besides testis and ovary, citing Evans et al., Endocrinology 2008. It is a signalling receptor with widespread low-level non-reproductive expression, not a germline-restricted gene.
best_source: Lin DC et al., J Biol Chem 2002;277(22):19276-80, PMID 11886876 (abstract only); see also Soga T et al., Biochim Biophys Acta 2002, PMID 12427552
verify_reason: UniProt Q8TCW9 does list this tissue panel, but it attributes it to Evans et al. 2008 (PMID 18339712), which is a decidua/early-pregnancy paper; a search of its open-access full text found none of pituitary, salivary, small intestine or spleen as an expression result. The list matches Lin et al., JBC 2002 (PMID 11886876), whose abstract says prokineticin receptor mRNA is 'expressed in gastrointestinal organs, endocrine glands, and other tissues'. A second cloning paper (Soga 2002, PMID 12427552) reports a different PK-R1 distribution (testis, medulla oblongata, skeletal muscle, skin) and notes PK-R1 and PK-R2 are 87% identical, so paralog cross-detection in these 2002 RT-PCR tissue panels cannot be excluded from the abstracts alone. The evidence is bulk mRNA only, with no cell type, no quantitation and no protein outside decidua, so it does not contradict the atlas maximum of 1.6 TPM. Real low-level non-reproductive expression is plausible but weaker and less well sourced than claimed. I did not check mouse knockout literature.
criteria_gap: The atlas maximum is 1.6 TPM in adipose, below the screen threshold, so the gene passes on RNA level alone. A low-abundance GPCR can be functional at that level, and the expression is probably confined to rare enteric or endothelial cells. Pituitary, adrenal and salivary gland may be weakly covered. Mouse knockout phenotypes could not be checked this session.

claim: Rat (SHR model): a review states Sry is expressed in brain, kidney and adrenal gland of adult males and links the Sry locus to blood-pressure regulation via the sympathetic and renin-angiotensin systems. Rat carries multiple Sry copies, so transfer to human is uncertain.
best_source: PMID 19914267 (PMC2891862), Ely et al., Steroids 2010 (rat review)
verify_reason: Source exists and says it: abstract of PMID 19914267 (Ely et al., Steroids 2010) states Sry 'is expressed in the brain, kidney and adrenal gland of adult males' and links the SHR Y chromosome/Sry locus to blood pressure via the sympathetic and renin-angiotensin systems. But it is a review of rat work (SHR/WKY), the rat has multiple functional Sry copies (stated in the abstract) so the data are about a multi-copy locus with no one-to-one human orthologue, and the hypertension model is a disease strain. The only human content is Y-chromosome association with blood pressure, not SRY expression in kidney or adrenal. No human adult kidney/adrenal expression is shown. The finding was already framed as rat-only and 'possible'; that is accurate, and it does not bear on human normal-tissue expression beyond the brain claim covered separately.
criteria_gap: Rodent-only functional evidence for adult non-reproductive expression; human bulk RNA is near zero in these tissues and no literature verdict exists for the gene.

tissue: brain, spinal cord, dorsal root ganglia
cell_type: neurons and glia (hippocampal pyramidal layer, Purkinje cells)
claim: Rat only: StarD6 immunoreactivity in multiple neuronal and glial populations of brain, spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia (PMID 17885612), mainly stratum pyramidale of hippocampus (PMID 20609383), with transient induction after pilocarpine seizures (PMID 19434006) and domoic acid excitotoxicity (PMID 22883302). All from one group using antibody-based assays; no human data found.
verify_reason: All four PMIDs exist and say what is claimed, but every one is rat, from one group, using antibody immunoreactivity or western blot without knockout validation. PMID 20609383 itself says the characteristics 'are in controversy'. No human data; UniProt P59095 has no tissue-specificity entry.
criteria_gap: Protein-level and injury-induced expression despite low RNA; the CSV's off-target maximum is blood (0.66 TPM) and human brain RNA is low, so this is either a species difference or antibody cross-reactivity.

claim: UniProt states that TTLL13 is a tubulin polyglutamylase that, with CFAP100, glutamylates spindle-pole microtubules and is needed for proper spindle assembly (PMID 40593606, cited on both the human A6NNM8 and mouse A4Q9F6 entries). Mouse Ttll13 expression is reported highest in heart and testis.
source: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A6NNM8 and https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A4Q9F6 (cite PMID 40593606; paper not opened)
best_source: PMID 40593606 (Sun et al., Nat Commun 2025;16:5591, PMC12219730); mouse tissue RT-PCR in PMID 17499049 and ependymal cilia in PMID 23897886 via UniProt A4Q9F6
verify_reason: The UniProt statements are as claimed on both A6NNM8 and A4Q9F6. I opened the cited paper (Sun et al., Nat Commun 2025, PMC12219730), which answers the researcher's open question: the spindle-pole evidence is from the HaCaT immortalised human keratinocyte line, HEK293T and HeLa cells, plus primary keratinocytes from mice. It is not from normal adult human tissue. The knockout in the paper is Cfap100, not Ttll13; TTLL13 evidence is co-immunoprecipitation of the endogenous protein in HaCaT, localisation of TTLL13-GFP (and TTLL13 in mouse primary keratinocytes) at spindle poles, and rescue by TTLL13 overexpression. So endogenous TTLL13 protein is detected by antibody in a human keratinocyte line, which is suggestive for dividing epidermal cells but is cell-line evidence with no TTLL13 loss-of-function. Mouse heart expression (PMID 17499049) is mouse RT-PCR only. Skin is already in the bulk panel.
criteria_gap: A mitotic spindle role would mean cell-cycle-restricted expression in proliferating normal cells (bone marrow, gut crypts, activated lymphocytes), which steady-state bulk RNA at 1.6 TPM does not resolve. Whether the spindle evidence comes from normal somatic cells or from cell lines or germ cells was not verified because the paper was not opened.

tissue: brain, kidney, liver (mouse); also heart, lung, muscle, spleen
claim: Mouse Ttll2 (UniProt A4Q9E4) is reported as most highly expressed in brain, kidney, liver and testis, with lower expression in heart, lung, muscle and spleen (PMID 17499049). The human entry (Q9BWV7) says only that it is testis-expressed.
best_source: UniProt A4Q9E4 citing PMID 17499049 (van Dijk et al., Mol Cell 2007;26:437); human UniProt Q9BWV7 lists testis only
verify_reason: UniProt A4Q9E4 (mouse) says exactly this, citing PMID 17499049 (van Dijk et al., Mol Cell 2007), and the human entry Q9BWV7 lists tissue specificity as 'Testis' only. The evidence is mouse RT-PCR across tissues from a single paper whose abstract confirms differential tissue expression of the polyglutamylases; the full text is not open access and I did not read the expression figure itself. There is no human data, no protein-level data, no knockout phenotype, and the enzyme activity is annotated only as 'probable'. The human annotation directly disagrees with broad somatic expression, so this is most likely a species difference or low-level RT-PCR signal, not evidence of a human normal-tissue function.
criteria_gap: Human off-target RNA is already the highest in this batch (6.55 TPM in blood, 1.6 nTPM); the mouse gene-specific data suggest broader somatic expression than the human atlases show, and the protein has no literature verdict in the catalog. Mouse-only evidence, possibly a species difference.

tissue: brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, spleen, trachea (mouse)
cell_type: ciliated cells implied by function (cilia glycylation)
claim: Mouse Ttll8 (UniProt A4Q9F1) is a tubulin monoglycylase that, with TTLL3, glycylates cilia as well as sperm flagella; expression is highest in testis but also reported in brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, spleen and trachea. The Ttll3/Ttll8 double knockout phenotype listed is subfertility from abnormal flagellar beating (PMID 33414192), so no vital somatic phenotype is documented.
source: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A4Q9F1 (cites PMID 33414192 and others; papers not opened)
best_source: UniProt A4Q9F1 tissue specificity citing PMID 23897886 (ependymal cilia), PMID 17499049 and PMID 25180231; knockout PMID 33414192 (Gadadhar et al., Science 2021)
verify_reason: UniProt A4Q9F1 (mouse) does say this: highly expressed in testis, also expressed in brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, spleen and trachea, and in brain specifically in ependymal cilia (PMID 23897886), and the Ttll3/Ttll8 double knockout is subfertile (PMID 33414192, abstract confirms a male fertility phenotype only). All of it is mouse. The human entry A6PVC2 has no tissue annotation and its function text is inferred by similarity from the mouse protein. The mouse data are gene-specific RT-PCR, but the only knockout phenotype is reproductive, so no vital somatic role is documented. The ependymal-cilia detail strengthens the researcher's point that a rare-ciliated-cell signal could be diluted in bulk, but it remains an unverified possibility in human.
criteria_gap: Human bulk RNA peaks at 0.41 TPM, but a cilia-restricted enzyme in rare multiciliated cells (airway, ependyma) would be diluted in bulk tissue, and trachea and ependyma are not in the rare-cell screen's tissue list. Mouse-only evidence; human UniProt entry has no tissue annotation.

tissue: blood / hematopoietic cells (also brain, liver, muscle by Northern)
claim: Human, family-level: the near-identical USP17 copy DUB-3 (USP17L2) is transiently induced by IL-4 and IL-6, and Northern blotting detected transcripts in brain, liver and muscle. UniProt also records protein-level up-regulation by IL-4, IL-6, CXCL8 and CXCL12 and at the G1/S transition; the probes cannot distinguish the tandem-repeat copies, so this may apply to USP17L1.
best_source: PMID 14699124 (DUB-3/USP17L2); UniProt Q6R6M4 induction annotation citing PMID 14699124, 20388806, 21448158
verify_reason: PMID 14699124 exists and its abstract says what is claimed, but about DUB-3 (USP17L2), not USP17L1: Northern signal in brain, liver and muscle, and induction by IL-4 and IL-6. The induction and the anti-proliferative effect are reported alongside tumour cell lines and murine Ba/F3 and NIH3T3 cells; the abstract shows no induction in normal primary human hematopoietic cells. The Northern probe cannot separate the tandem-repeat copies. UniProt's induction annotation sits on the USP17L2 entry (Q6R6M4); the USP17L1 entry (Q7RTZ2) has no tissue or induction annotation. Family-level inference only.
criteria_gap: Steady-state bulk and single-cell RNA cannot see transient cytokine- or cell-cycle-induced expression, and multi-mapping reads across the USP17L tandem repeat are under-counted (mapping_risk is True). COVERAGE CAVEAT FOR THIS WHOLE BATCH: the session web-search budget ran out after one search, so all 25 labels were checked only against UniProt curated annotations and the PubMed abstracts UniProt cites; absence of a finding for the other labels is weaker than a full literature search.

claim: Human: deletion mapping in 15 males with Xp22.3 deletions narrowed an X-linked nonspecific mental retardation interval to about 15 kb containing only VCX-A (VCX3A); it was deleted in all patients with mental retardation and retained in all with normal intelligence. This implies a neurodevelopmental or brain role, although UniProt still lists expression as exclusively testis and the paralogues VCX, VCX2 and VCX3B showed no such correlation.
best_source: PMID 18076704 and PMID 18194880 (contradicting follow-ups); original claim PMID 10903929
verify_reason: PMID 10903929 exists, is specific to VCX-A (VCX3A) and says what is claimed: a 15 kb critical interval, deleted in all patients with mental retardation and retained in all with normal intelligence. But it is deletion mapping, not evidence of expression in adult brain, and later studies contradict it. PMID 18076704 found VCX3A deleted in 62 of 80 X-linked ichthyosis patients with normal intelligence and concluded the deletion is not sufficient for mental retardation. PMID 18194880 reports a male with all VCX genes and NLGN4X deleted and normal intelligence. UniProt lists expression as exclusively testis. Any role would be developmental, and the causal link is disputed.
criteria_gap: The screen has no human-genetics input, and VCX3A has no literature verdict. Brain RNA is near zero (0.4 TPM thalamus), so any role may be developmental or in rare cells, and paralogue multi-mapping (mapping_risk True) could hide low expression.

claim: Human: the VHL-like protein cDNA was originally isolated by RT-PCR from human cerebellum (and cancer cell lines), with the transcript most abundant in placenta; the protein binds HIF-alpha and acts as a dominant-negative VHL. This gene-specific cloning supports the catalog's 4.4 TPM cerebellum value being real expression rather than mis-mapped VHL reads.
verify_reason: PMID 14757845 exists and its abstract states a 676-bp partial cDNA was isolated by RT-PCR from human brain cerebellum and several cancer cell lines, with the transcript most abundant in placenta. That is qualitative detection by PCR cloning with no quantification and no protein evidence; the abstract does not state donor age or status. The cloned product was sequenced (78% similar to VHL), so it is distinct from VHL, though VHLL is an intronless retrogene and genomic DNA contamination cannot be excluded from the abstract. It supports low-level cerebellar transcript presence, not a documented function in adult brain; the dominant-negative VHL function was shown by overexpression.
criteria_gap: VHLL is categorised 'Cancer Antigen only' with no literature verdict and sits below the rare-cell screen; the cerebellar signal is below the bulk threshold but is independently confirmed by RT-PCR cloning.

cell_type: hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons; dentate gyrus polymorphic layer
claim: Human: ZACN (L2/ZAC, zinc-activated ligand-gated cation channel) cDNA was cloned from adult caudate nucleus; RT-PCR confirmed mRNA in adult hippocampus, striatum, amygdala and thalamus, and an antipeptide antibody stained protein mainly in hippocampal CA3 pyramidal cells and the dentate gyrus polymorphic layer. The same tissue cDNA panels also detected mRNA in pancreas, liver, lung, heart, kidney and skeletal muscle.
best_source: PMID 16083862 (primary); PMID 33962015 for the statement that in vivo protein expression is not consistently demonstrated
verify_reason: The source exists and its abstract says what is claimed: L2/ZAC cDNA cloned from human caudate nucleus, RT-PCR mRNA in adult hippocampus, striatum, amygdala and thalamus, plus brain, pancreas, liver, lung, heart, kidney and skeletal muscle on tissue cDNA panels, and antipeptide-antibody staining in hippocampal CA3 pyramidal cells and the dentate gyrus polymorphic layer. ZACN has no close paralog (about 15% identity to 5-HT3A/B), so the RT-PCR is gene-specific. The protein part is weaker than 'documented': the abstract itself calls it 'L2-like immunoreactivity' from a single unvalidated antipeptide antibody, and the main ZAC laboratory wrote in 2021 (PMID 33962015) that 'expression of the ZAC protein in vivo has yet to be consistently demonstrated'. The RT-PCR is non-quantitative and agrees with the low atlas RNA. I read only the abstract (full text is paywalled), so the species of the stained sections is confirmed only through a later paper (PMID 26872532) that describes them as human. No physiological function or loss-of-function phenotype is known. Net: gene-specific low-level brain RNA is real; neuronal protein expression is unconfirmed.
criteria_gap: Bulk RNA is low everywhere (CSV maximum 3.7 TPM in colon) and the rare-cell screen is 'below_screen', so a functional ion channel with gene-specific RT-PCR and antibody evidence in specific hippocampal neurons passes. This protein was not among the roughly 99 given a literature review. The antibody is a single antipeptide reagent from 2005, not knockout-validated. COVERAGE CAVEAT FOR THE WHOLE BATCH: the session's web search budget was exhausted before any search ran, so every protein here was checked only against its UniProt entry (function, tissue specificity, induction, disease, cited papers) plus four PubMed abstracts; no free-text literature search was done for any of the 25.

claim: Human: the original cloning paper detected ZAC transcripts in adult trachea, spinal cord and stomach (plus placenta and fetal brain), and showed the expressed channel is functional (spontaneous currents, activated by Zn2+, blocked by tubocurarine). The gene is absent from mouse and rat, so no rodent knockout exists to reveal a phenotype.
verify_reason: The source exists and the abstract states: 'Transcripts of ZAC subunits were detected in human placenta, trachea, spinal cord, stomach, and fetal brain', the gene is lost from mouse and rat, and the HEK293-expressed channel shows spontaneous current, Zn2+ activation and tubocurarine block. All of that matches the claim. Weakened because: the abstract does not say the trachea, spinal cord and stomach samples were adult (likely commercial adult RNA panels, but I did not verify this in the full text); detection is qualitative with no level, cell type or protein; channel function is shown only in transfected cells, not native tissue; and no physiological role or human loss-of-function phenotype is known. The rodent-orthologue point is correct. This is gene-specific evidence of low-level transcript, not a documented function in these tissues.
criteria_gap: Trachea and spinal cord are thin or absent in the bulk panels, and the donor-level rare-cell screen does not cover airway beyond lung or spinal cord. The lack of a rodent orthologue means mouse knockout evidence cannot be used to clear this gene.

claim: Human: the cloning paper states CYP26C1 is not widely expressed in the adult but is inducible by retinoic acid in a transformed human keratinocyte line. It is a functional retinoic-acid-catabolising enzyme. Biallelic loss causes focal facial dermal dysplasia type IV (PMID 29263414), a congenital developmental skin defect, which is an expected embryonic role and not counted as a finding.
source: PMID 14532297 (Taimi et al., J Biol Chem 2004, doi:10.1074/jbc.M308337200)
best_source: PMID 14532297 (Taimi et al., J Biol Chem 2004, doi:10.1074/jbc.M308337200)
verify_reason: Source exists and the abstract says exactly this: 'CYP26C1 is not widely expressed in the adult but is inducible by RA in HPK1a, transformed human keratinocyte cell lines.' The evidence is a transformed (HPV-immortalised) cell line treated with exogenous retinoic acid in vitro, not normal adult skin in vivo; the same sentence actually supports low adult expression. Paralog specificity is not established from the abstract (CYP26A1/B1 are also RA-inducible in keratinocytes), though the cloning paper presumably used CYP26C1-specific probes. Not evidence of normal-tissue expression.
criteria_gap: Retinoid-induced expression would not appear in steady-state atlases, and skin is not in the rare-cell screen. The evidence is from a transformed cell line only, with no in vivo adult skin data, so relevance is limited mainly to patients on retinoid therapy.

claim: Human IL36B (IL-1F8) is an inducible pro-inflammatory cytokine: IL-1A and TNF induce it in human keratinocytes, and IL-1A, IL-1B and TNF induce it in synovial fibroblasts (UniProt curated induction, citing Magne 2006). Reviews found in search also report induction in keratinocytes by IL-17A, TNF and IL-36 itself, with keratinocytes the main source in psoriatic plaques.
source: PMID 16646978 (abstract read; induction details from the UniProt IL36B entry); review https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2019.01162/full
best_source: PMID 21881584 (Carrier et al., J Invest Dermatol 2011) for keratinocyte induction; PMID 16646978 / PMC1526623 for synovial fibroblasts only
verify_reason: The cited paper (Magne 2006, PMID 16646978) exists but does not test keratinocytes: per its full text (PMC1526623) the cells studied were human synovial fibroblasts, articular chondrocytes, dermal fibroblasts and cell lines. It does show IL-1F8 mRNA induction by IL-1beta/TNF/IL-1alpha in cultured human synovial fibroblasts from joint-replacement patients, but IL-1F8 protein was undetectable in supernatants and not raised in inflamed joint tissue. The keratinocyte statement comes from the UniProt induction line, which misattributes it to this paper. Keratinocyte induction is real but is better supported by Carrier 2011 (cultured primary human keratinocytes, IL-17A and TNF), which is in vitro and psoriatic-lesion evidence, not normal adult tissue. UniProt itself says healthy control skin is low. The Frontiers review was not opened.
criteria_gap: All RNA panels are steady-state healthy tissue. The 7.5 TPM skin value understates expression in inflamed, wounded or infected skin, where target-directed therapy would meet induced antigen on keratinocytes. Nothing in the screen models inducible expression.

cell_type: CD4+ regulatory T cells (Foxp3+), anergic CD4 T cells
claim: Mouse: Izumo1R (FOLR4/FR4) is a surface protein on CD4+ T cells, highest on Tregs under Foxp3 control; Treg-specific knockout causes subclinical skin inflammation and susceptibility to imiquimod-induced, gamma-delta T cell-driven dermatitis (PMID 36972453). FR4 is also a marker shared by Tregs and anergic CD4 T cells (PMID 28320913). No human Treg expression data were found in this session.
verify_reason: Both sources exist and say what is claimed, but in mouse only. PMID 36972453 abstract: Izumo1R is expressed in CD4 T cells, especially Tregs under Foxp3 control; Treg-specific knockout gives subclinical skin inflammation and unique susceptibility to imiquimod-induced, gamma-delta T cell-dependent disease. PMID 28320913 abstract: anergic CD4 T cells and Tregs share folate receptor 4 expression. The knockout is gene-specific. No human Treg evidence was found: UniProt A6ND01 lists human expression only in unfertilized oocytes, and a PubMed query returned nothing relevant. I could not run a web search for human data (search budget exhausted), so absence of human evidence is not established.
criteria_gap: The sorted immune-cell bulk panels and the rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut) do not resolve Tregs or activated/anergic T cells specifically; surface protein on a small immune subset would not register in bulk TPM. Mouse-only, so human relevance is unconfirmed.

tissue: skin epidermis; oral and oesophageal epithelium
claim: Human: as for LCE3C. LCE3B is a cornified-envelope component detected by quantitative PCR in adult skin, tongue and oesophagus (PMID 15854049), induced in normal epidermis by barrier disruption (de Cid 2009), with antibacterial activity (PMID 28634035). It is deleted together with LCE3C in the common psoriasis risk allele.
verify_reason: Same evidence as LCE3C. The sources are real and human, but induction on barrier disruption is reported for LCE/LCE3 genes as a group in the de Cid 2009 abstract, the protein evidence is a pan-LCE3 antibody, and the antibacterial activity is for LCE3 proteins with LCE3A most active. Jackson 2005 describes the group as low-level in barrier epithelia; per-gene LCE3B values in tongue and oesophagus were not verified from the abstract. Strong expression is in injured or psoriatic skin rather than resting normal skin, and the gene is commonly homozygously deleted in healthy people.
criteria_gap: Induced on barrier injury, so resting-tissue bulk RNA (2.7 TPM, in a disposable tissue) understates expression in wounded or inflamed skin. Skin is not in the rare-cell screen.

tissue: skin epidermis; oral and oesophageal epithelium
claim: Human: LCE3 genes are induced in normal epidermis by skin barrier disruption and strongly expressed in psoriatic lesions (de Cid 2009). Quantitative PCR also detects LCE3B/3C in adult skin, tongue and oesophagus with group-wise response to calcium and UV (PMID 15854049), a pan-LCE3 monoclonal antibody stains suprabasal epidermis (PMID 26556599), and LCE3 proteins have defensin-like antibacterial activity (PMID 28634035). Homozygous LCE3B/C deletion is a common psoriasis risk allele in healthy people, so the gene is dispensable.
best_source: PMID 19169253 (induction, group-level); PMID 15854049 (group-specific qPCR); PMID 26556599 (pan-LCE3 antibody)
verify_reason: The sources exist and are human. The de Cid 2009 abstract says 'LCE expression can be induced in normal epidermis by skin barrier disruption and is strongly expressed in psoriatic lesions', which is LCE/LCE3-group wording and not specific to LCE3C. Jackson 2005 (PMID 15854049) describes the group-3 genes as 'low-level' in all barrier-forming epithelia including internal ones; I read only the abstract, so the per-gene tongue and oesophagus values are not verified. The antibody in PMID 26556599 is explicitly pan-LCE3, so it does not separate LCE3C from LCE3A/B/D/E. The antibacterial activity in PMID 28634035 is for LCE3 proteins, 'LCE3A in particular'. Induction is real at group level, but constitutive normal expression is low, the strong expression is in injured or psoriatic skin, and the homozygous deletion is common in healthy people.
criteria_gap: Expression is injury-induced rather than constitutive, so resting-skin bulk RNA understates it. Skin and oral mucosa are not in the rare-cell screen. The catalog's highest value (21.4 TPM) is in a disposable tissue and is therefore discounted, while the same squamous-epithelial programme operates in skin, tongue and oesophagus.

claim: Human keratinocytes express P2Y4 mRNA by RT-PCR with functional evidence in HaCaT cells; immunolabelling placed P2Y4 on the sarcolemma of human vastus lateralis fibres; a quantitative RT-PCR survey reported widespread, subtype-selective P2Y4 mRNA across human peripheral tissues and brain regions. UniProt lists pancreas, where the gene was cloned.
best_source: PMID 11690642; PMID 8617367 for the pancreas-restricted counter-evidence
verify_reason: All four sources exist. PMID 12603858: RT-PCR in cultured keratinocytes and HaCaT, with the functional P2Y4 signature seen only in a subpopulation of HaCaT cells, not in normal keratinocytes. PMID 22052557: antibody labelling of vastus lateralis sarcolemma, no specificity control mentioned in the abstract. PMID 11690642: qRT-PCR survey reporting widespread expression. PMID 8617367 contradicts the breadth, reporting expression exclusively in pancreas, and states the gene is intronless, so RT-PCR signal can come from genomic DNA unless controlled. Cultured cells and antibodies, not normal tissue in situ.
criteria_gap: Gene-specific qRT-PCR and antibody data suggest broader low-level expression than atlas thresholds register; antibody specificity for P2Y receptors is often poor, so this is graded possible.

claim: Human: UniProt's tissue-specificity annotation (citing the original cloning paper, PMID 9047241) lists expression in kidney, brain and skin in addition to testis. The large 2022 IHC study (PMID 35973038) found kidney, brain and adrenal negative at protein level, so this is low-level RNA not confirmed as protein; a search summary also indicated adrenocortical staining varies by antibody clone, but I did not open that source.
best_source: PMID 35973038 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9588667/) for protein-level negatives; UniProt P78395 citing PMID 9047241 for the RNA statement
verify_reason: UniProt P78395 does say 'Expressed in testis. Detected in samples of kidney, brain and skin', citing PMID 9047241. I could not open the Ikeda 1997 full text (publisher returned 403); its abstract says only 'expressed ... in some normal tissues, albeit at a lower level'. Secondary reviews of that paper name testis, adrenal, ovary and endometrium as the normal sites, not kidney, brain or skin, so those three rest on the UniProt curation alone and I marked the adult/normal and gene-specific flags from that annotation, not from the paper. The 2022 IHC study on 70 normal tissues found kidney, brain and adrenal negative, and skin negative apart from sebaceous glands. At most this is trace RNA without protein, as the flagger concedes. The 'adrenocortical staining varies by clone' remark is unsourced and should be disregarded.
criteria_gap: The catalog records only adrenal as the top off-target tissue (3.0 TPM, 20.3 nTPM). Gene-specific RNA in kidney, brain and skin is low and contradicted by IHC, so this argues for keeping PRAME rather than removing it.

tissue: skin / connective tissue (primary fibroblasts); broad tissues
claim: Human/primate: the SPATA31A/C family 'broadened the expression into many tissues' relative to the testis-only mouse gene; antibody staining shows the protein in human fibroblast nucleoli with relocalisation to the whole nucleus after UV, and CRISPR reduction of SPATA31A copies in human primary fibroblasts increased UV sensitivity. Antibody and knockout are family-level, so this applies to the SPATA31A copies in the batch (A1, A3, A5, A6, A7), not demonstrably to the D or F subfamilies.
source: PMID 28264649 (Bekpen et al., BMC Genomics 2017); related PMID 29676996
best_source: PMID 28264649 (PMC5338094), Bekpen et al., BMC Genomics 2017
verify_reason: Source exists and the abstract of PMID 28264649 (Bekpen et al., BMC Genomics 2017) says the family 'broadened the expression into many tissues', that the protein relocalises from nucleolus to whole nucleus after UV, and that CRISPR reduction of copies in human primary fibroblasts increased UV sensitivity. PMID 29676996 exists but is about SPATA31A1 overexpression causing premature senescence and copy number versus longevity, not normal-tissue expression. Weaknesses on full-text check (PMC5338094): (1) not gene-specific: the RT-PCR/qPCR detects A and C types together, and the antibody was raised against peptides shared by A and C types, with western bands at 170-200 kD versus 157/130 kD predicted; nothing distinguishes SPATA31A1 from A3/A5/A6/A7 or the C copies. (2) Expression outside testis is described by the authors as 'quite low' with testis still highest, from commercial pooled total RNA (brain, liver, kidney, heart, lung, thymus, spleen, cerebellum) with no donor/age details. (3) The functional evidence is in cultured HFF foreskin fibroblast lines (ATCC CRL-2703/CRL-2450), i.e. in vitro cells of neonatal-type origin, not adult tissue in situ. (4) The only tissue IHC (lung and sinus epithelium, tonsil) uses sections labelled 'Lung CF' and 'Tonsil allergic', i.e. apparently diseased tissue, with the same family-level antibody and no quantification. Real family-level signal that the atlases cannot exclude because of multi-mapping, but it is not demonstrated for SPATA31A1 specifically nor in normal adult tissue.
criteria_gap: These are multi-copy, mapping-risk genes whose RNA-seq reads are multi-mapped and reported as ~0 TPM, so the atlases cannot exclude low somatic expression; the function is a UV-damage response (induced relocalisation, stress context) in fibroblasts, which no bulk, single-cell or IHC criterion tests. No literature review was done for the family.

claim: Human: TAS2R1 (with TAS2R38) protein was shown by double immunostaining with alpha-gustducin in human skin, HaCaT cells and primary keratinocytes; bitter agonists triggered calcium influx and raised differentiation markers (keratin 10, involucrin, transglutaminase).
best_source: PMID 25573083 (Wolfle et al. 2015, Skin Pharmacol Physiol)
verify_reason: PMID 25573083 exists and its abstract says what is claimed: TAS2R1 and TAS2R38 expression in human skin, colocalisation with alpha-gustducin in HaCaT cells and primary keratinocytes, and calcium influx and differentiation markers after diphenidol or amarogentin. Weakened because the protein evidence is antibody immunostaining only (TAS2R antibodies are not knockout-validated in the abstract), the functional work is mostly in the HaCaT line, and the agonists are promiscuous across TAS2Rs, so the function is not attributable to TAS2R1 specifically. I read the abstract only, not the full text.
criteria_gap: The catalog's highest off-target value is brain (basal ganglia) and the existing literature verdict covers specialised tissue; skin keratinocyte protein with low RNA is not captured by bulk TPM thresholds, and skin is not in the donor-level rare-cell screen.

claim: Human: siRNA knockdown of TCHHL1 in normal human keratinocytes reduced proliferation and increased early apoptosis, and skin-equivalent models built from knockdown cells had a hypoplastic epidermis.
verify_reason: PMID 33133644 (Makino et al., Cell Death Discov 2020) exists and its abstract states the claim as written: TCHHL1 siRNA inhibited proliferation and induced early apoptosis of normal human keratinocytes, and skin-equivalent models built from knockdown cells had a markedly hypoplastic epidermis. The siRNA is gene-specific. It is weakened because the evidence is entirely in vitro (cultured primary keratinocytes and 3D skin equivalents, which are often of neonatal origin), not adult tissue in vivo, and there is no human loss-of-function disease or mouse knockout. Same laboratory as the other TCHHL1 papers; abstract only was read.
criteria_gap: The screen has no functional evidence layer for this gene (no literature verdict), and low bulk RNA hides a functional role in the proliferating epidermal compartment.

claim: Human skin xenotransplants: UVB irradiation raised TCHHL1 mRNA two days after exposure, and immunohistochemistry showed the signal spreading from the basal into the spinous layer.
verify_reason: PMID 30610764 (Makino et al., Clin Exp Dermatol 2019) exists and its abstract matches the claim: TCHHL1 mRNA rose 2 days after UVB, and immunohistochemistry signal spread from the basal layer (sham) into basal and spinous layers, alongside more Ki67-positive cells. Weakened because the tissue is human skin grafted onto mice, not skin in a person, and the abstract gives no fold change. The induction tracks keratinocyte proliferation, so it is an extension of the basal-layer finding rather than an independent one. Abstract only was read.
criteria_gap: Expression is induced by UV exposure; atlas skin samples are resting-state, so constitutive RNA thresholds understate it.

claim: Human: whole-transcriptome analysis of foliate papillae swabs from hospital staff named OR1A2 among olfactory receptor transcripts detected in tongue taste tissue, with lower levels in subjects reporting sensory impairment after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
best_source: PMID 38965271 (Danzer et al. 2024, Sci Rep; PMC11224223)
verify_reason: Abstract confirmed: OR1A2 is named among 166 ORs with lower expression in IgG+/sensory-impaired hospital staff in foliate papillae swab transcriptomes. Adult human, non-reproductive, mostly healthy volunteers. But evidence is whole-transcriptome only (hybridisation/sequence-based, not validated per gene), from surface swabs of mixed cell composition (not confirmed taste cells), 166 ORs detected suggests low-level/background signal, and OR1A1 (close paralog) is listed alongside, so cross-mapping is not excluded. No protein or functional data. Only the abstract was verified by me.
criteria_gap: Taste epithelium is absent from the bulk HPA/GTEx panels and from the rare-cell screen tissues. Evidence is RNA only from a single swab-based study, read at abstract level.

claim: UniProt annotates human OR8D2 as expressed in the tongue and possibly involved in taste perception, based on a degenerate-primer RT-PCR screen of a human lingual cDNA library that recovered olfactory-like receptor transcripts from adult and fetal tongue.
verify_reason: UniProt Q9GZM6 confirms OR8D2 is the clone JCG2 and annotates 'Expressed in the tongue'. The PMID 11705801 abstract says the genes are expressed 'in adult tongue and/or in fetal tongue' and that all are expressed in fetal tongue; the ones named as expressed in adult tongue epithelium are HGMP071, HTPCR06, TPCR120, JCG3 and JCG5. JCG2 is not on that list, so only fetal expression is supported by the abstract. The assay is degenerate-primer RT-PCR on a cDNA library for a gene family that is typically intronless, so genomic carry-over is not excluded.
criteria_gap: Taste and lingual epithelium are not resolved by bulk panels. Evidence is a single 2001 RT-PCR study without quantification; the abstract does not name which clone corresponds to OR8D2, UniProt makes that link.

cell_type: type III acid-sensing (PKD2L1+) taste receptor cells
claim: OTOP1 is the proton channel that acts as the sour taste receptor; human OTOP1 conducts proton currents and senses ammonium chloride (UniProt Q7RTM1, PMID 29371428, 37798269). Protein localisation in sour taste cells and the loss of acid responses in knockouts are mouse data (PMID 31543453, 31543264).
best_source: PMID 31543453 (mouse Otop1 knockout, type III taste cells); PMID 37798269 for human channel activity in HEK-293
verify_reason: Sources exist and say what is claimed, but no cited source shows OTOP1 in human taste tissue. PMID 29371428 identifies murine OTOP1 in acid-detecting taste cells; PMID 37798269 shows human OTOP1 carries NH4Cl currents only when expressed in HEK-293 cells; PMID 31543453 and 31543264 are mouse knockouts. UniProt Q7RTM1 marks the sour-receptor role 'by similarity'. The assays are gene-specific (knockout, heterologous expression) and the function is very likely conserved, but the in-tissue evidence is mouse-only.
criteria_gap: Taste epithelium is absent from the bulk RNA panels and from the rare-cell screen (brain, eye, heart, lung, kidney, liver, pancreas, gut); taste cells are too rare to register in bulk tongue. NOTE for the whole batch: the session web-search budget was exhausted, so every finding here rests on direct UniProt, GeneRIF and PubMed-abstract fetches rather than open web search; coverage of the less-studied genes is correspondingly thinner.

claim: Human: UniProt curates TAS2R8 as a bitter taste receptor expressed in subsets of taste receptor cells of the tongue and palate epithelium, exclusively in gustducin-positive cells; it may also sense gastrointestinal contents.
best_source: PMID 18003842 (Behrens et al., J Neurosci 2007; PMCID PMC6673335)
verify_reason: UniProt Q9NYW2 does carry the quoted tissue-specificity text, but that sentence has no evidence tag and is identical word for word in the TAS2R9 entry: it is a family-level statement copied from the abstract of Adler et al. 2000 (PMID 10761934), whose in situ localisation and gustducin co-expression were done in rodent taste tissue. The companion paper PMID 10761935 characterised mT2R-5, hT2R-4 and mT2R-8 (a mouse gene, not human TAS2R8). The UniProt function line is hedged ('may play a role'), and the gastrointestinal role is speculative. So the cited source is not gene-specific human evidence. The underlying claim is nonetheless supported by a better source: Behrens et al. 2007 report all 25 human TAS2R genes expressed in taste receptor cells of human circumvallate papillae by in situ hybridisation with gene-specific probes (abstract read; per-gene levels for TAS2R8 not checked).
criteria_gap: Taste buds are a tiny fraction of bulk tongue and are not sampled by the bulk panels or the rare-cell screen, so a physiological receptor in adult taste cells reads as near-zero RNA.

claim: Human: UniProt curates TAS2R9 as a gustducin-coupled bitter taste receptor expressed in subsets of taste receptor cells of the tongue and palate epithelium; the gastrointestinal role is annotated by similarity only. Human TAS2R9 polymorphisms predict perceived bitterness of acesulfame potassium, supporting a working receptor in adults.
best_source: PMID 18003842 (Behrens et al., J Neurosci 2007) for expression; PMID 23599216 for function in adults
verify_reason: UniProt Q9NYW1 does carry the quoted text, but the tissue-specificity sentence is the same untagged family-level boilerplate as in TAS2R8, derived from rodent in situ data in Adler et al. 2000 (PMID 10761934), and the function line is 'by similarity'. PMID 23599216 (Allen et al., Chem Senses 2013) is real and gene-specific: TAS2R9 alleles predicted acesulfame-K bitterness in 108 adults, and the abstract also cites a TAS2R9 allele effect on ofloxacin response in vitro. That is a genetic association in living adults (possible linkage with neighbouring TAS2R genes in the chr12 cluster), not a tissue expression assay, so it supports a working receptor only indirectly. The claim is real but the cited expression evidence is weaker than stated; the direct human evidence is Behrens et al. 2007, in situ hybridisation of all 25 human TAS2R genes in human circumvallate papillae (abstract read; per-gene level for TAS2R9 not checked).
criteria_gap: Taste epithelium is not in the bulk panels or the rare-cell screen; the receptor is confined to a rare sensory cell type.

tissue: tooth and alveolar bone; also reported in brain, bone marrow, long bone and cartilage
cell_type: ameloblasts; bone-lining cells; glial cells; macrophages, megakaryocytes and some CD34+ marrow cells
claim: Mouse (15 weeks): AMELX mRNA by RT-qPCR and protein by western blot in mandibular alveolar and basal bone, with low and inconsistent RT-PCR signal in eye, ovary, tongue, heart, colon and kidney (Jacques 2014, PMID 24933156). That paper cites earlier immunohistochemistry reports of amelogenin in brain glial cells and hematopoietic cells (Deutsch 2006, PMID 16674683) and in long bone, cartilage and marrow stromal cells (Haze 2007, PMID 17393535); those two were seen only as citations and search snippets, and species was not confirmed.
verify_reason: Jacques 2014 (PMC4059656) exists and matches the claim, but it is entirely mouse. AMELX mRNA was found in mandibular alveolar and basal bone at 1 and 15 weeks, falling with age; protein was a roughly 26 kDa band in alveolar bone and near the detection limit in basal bone. Bone-section staining was in 1-week-old mice. Soft-tissue RT-PCR at 15 weeks was low or inconsistent (eye and ovary positive; tongue, testicle, heart, colon, kidney inconsistent; liver, lung, muscle negative). No human tissue was studied. The paper cites Deutsch 2006 and Haze 2007 without stating species; I could not open either abstract (PubMed rate-limited), so the brain, hematopoietic, long bone and cartilage claims remain unverified. Mouse has no Amely, so the mouse data are gene-specific there, but the human AMELX/AMELY distinction is unaddressed and the antibodies are cross-species.
criteria_gap: Tooth, jaw bone, cartilage and bone marrow stroma are absent from the bulk panels and the rare-cell screen. The non-dental reports are low-level, mostly rodent and antibody-based, so they are suggestive rather than established for adult human tissue. Row is flagged mapping_risk (AMELX/AMELY homology).

claim: In adult mouse brain, Hes3 marks putative neural stem/progenitor cells in the SVZ, the dentate subgranular zone and the parenchyma. Its expression changes with demyelination/remyelination and metabolic insults, and Hes3-null neural stem cell cultures fail to respond to Delta4 or insulin. Mouse only.
source: doi:10.1038/s41598-018-29434-2 (found in search results; also PMC3518467 and Toutouna et al. 2016 Brain Research)
verify_reason: The DOI resolves to PMID 30054579 (Nikolakopoulou et al., Sci Rep 2018), an adult mouse brain study. Its abstract supports only that streptozotocin beta-cell damage, high-fat diet and metformin regulate Hes3 levels in mouse brain, and that Hes3 is expressed in neural stem and progenitor cells. The specific anatomical sites, the demyelination/remyelination changes and the Hes3-null culture result are not in this abstract and would rest on the other papers named, which I did not open. Entirely mouse, as the claim itself says; no human adult evidence.
criteria_gap: A rare, quiescent stem-cell population is diluted in bulk brain RNA (cerebral cortex 1.0 TPM) and may fall below the rare-cell screen threshold. Injury-induced expression is not modelled. Evidence is mouse-only.

claim: Mouse (review): Osx is expressed in odontoblasts and cementoblasts from late embryonic to postnatal stages, and odontoblast-specific conditional knockout gives short, thin tooth roots. Evidence is for postnatal root formation, not shown for mature adult teeth.
best_source: PMID 26599722 (He 2016, Int Endod J), a review of mouse primary studies
verify_reason: PMID 26599722 is a review and says what is claimed: Osx expression from late embryonic to postnatal stages in odontoblasts and cementoblasts, and odontoblast conditional knockout mice with short, thin roots. It is mouse, developmental/postnatal root formation, and a review rather than primary data; nothing about mature adult human teeth. The only human hint is delayed tooth eruption in the OI patient (PMID 20579626).
criteria_gap: Tooth is not in any bulk, IHC or single-cell panel used by the screen.

claim: Human, family-level: 11 of 17 high glycine-tyrosine KAP genes on 21q22.1 were expressed in the hair-forming compartment (Rogers 2002); member-level result not in the abstract. UniProt Q3LI60 is 'inferred from homology', so this member may be among the unexpressed ones.
best_source: none found; UniProt Q3LI60 has no expression data
verify_reason: The cited source very likely does not cover this gene. Rogers 2002 describes 17 high glycine-tyrosine genes in KAP6-8 and KAP19-22; my recollection of the member list (6.1-6.3, 7.1, 8.1, 19.1-19.7, 20.1-20.2, 21.1-21.2, 22.1) accounts for all 17, leaving no room for KAP20.3, which was annotated later. This is arithmetic from the abstract plus memory, not a read of the full text (publisher returned 403). UniProt Q3LI60 has no tissue annotation and is 'Inferred from homology'. No expression evidence found for this gene.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle is not sampled; per-gene result needs the full text.

claim: Human, family-level: 11 of 17 high glycine-tyrosine KAP genes on 21q22.1 were expressed in the hair-forming compartment (Rogers 2002); member-level result not in the abstract. UniProt Q3LI62 is 'inferred from homology'.
best_source: none found; UniProt Q3LI62 has no expression data
verify_reason: Same as KRTAP20-3: the 17 high glycine-tyrosine genes of Rogers 2002 appear to be fully accounted for by other members (KAP20 family = 20.1 and 20.2 only, by my recollection), so the paper's expression data do not apply to KAP20.4. Inferred from the abstract count; full text not accessible. UniProt Q3LI62 has no tissue annotation and is 'Inferred from homology'. No expression evidence found.
criteria_gap: Hair follicle is not sampled; per-gene result needs the full text.

claim: Human, family-level: 11 of 17 high glycine-tyrosine KAP genes on 21q22.1 were expressed in the hair-forming compartment (Rogers 2002); member-level result not in the abstract. UniProt Q3LHN1 is 'inferred from homology'.
best_source: none found; UniProt Q3LHN1 has no expression data
verify_reason: The 17 high glycine-tyrosine genes of Rogers 2002 appear fully accounted for by other members (KAP21 family = 21.1 and 21.2 only, by my recollection), so KAP21.3 is probably not among the genes assayed. claim: Human: Kouprina et al. report that SPANX-N genes, unlike SPANX-A/D, are expressed at a low level in several nongametogenic adult tissues, attributed to lower promoter CpG methylation. The abstract does not name the tissues or resolve individual SPANX-N members; the full text was not read.
verify_reason: Full text of PMID 17406683 (PMC1831492) read. RT-PCR used pan-SPANX-N primers, then products were cloned and sequenced to assign members (Table 2). For SPANX-N1 the only positive normal tissues were testis and cervix; prostate, placenta, lung, colon, brain, liver, muscle, spleen, heart, kidney and lymph node were negative. Only 4 of 120 clones from normal tissues were N1, while 95 of 103 clones from tumors and cancer lines were N1. Cervix is a reproductive-tract tissue, so there is no non-reproductive normal expression for this member; the family-level abstract statement does not apply to N1. The paper also notes N1 has a frameshift in exon 2.
criteria_gap: Flagged mapping_risk; near-identical SPANX-N paralogs can lose multi-mapped reads in bulk RNA-seq, so gene-specific RT-PCR reporting low somatic expression is not visible in the TPM values (0.24 TPM blood).

cell_type: cortical pyramidal neurons, hippocampal CA3/CA2 neurons, pinealocytes
claim: Mouse, disputed: Kim et al. (PNAS 2010) reported the enzyme as an aspartate racemase present in cortical and hippocampal neurons and pinealocytes, with knockdown impairing adult hippocampal neurogenesis. A later knockout study (Tanaka-Hayashi et al., Amino Acids 2015) found Got1l1 mRNA high in testis but not detected in brain, no racemase activity, and unchanged D-aspartate in knockout hippocampus. The weight of evidence favours testis-restricted expression.
verify_reason: Both sources exist and are described accurately, but together they refute brain expression rather than support it. Kim et al., PNAS 2010 (PMID 20133766) reported a cloned mammalian aspartate racemase that colocalizes with D-aspartate in brain and neuroendocrine tissues, with shRNA depletion in adult hippocampal newborn neurons impairing dendritic development and survival; this rests on antibody staining and shRNA, both prone to off-target effects. Tanaka-Hayashi et al., Amino Acids 2015 (PMID 25287256), using a Got1l1 knockout, found the mRNA 'highly expressed in the testis, but it is not detected in the brain and submandibular gland', no difference in D-aspartate between wild-type and knockout testis or hippocampus, and recombinant Got1l1 with aminotransferase but no racemase activity. The gene-specific knockout evidence agrees with the low human brain RNA. All data are mouse. The finding's own text concedes it is not a real screen gap; it should not count as normal-tissue expression. The cortex/CA3/pinealocyte localisation detail was not checked (abstracts only; PMC full text blocked by captcha).
criteria_gap: Not a real gap in the screen: the low brain RNA (0.9 TPM amygdala, 2.0 nTPM) agrees with the later knockout study. Recorded so a curator who meets the 2010 brain claim knows it has been contradicted by gene-specific work.

claim: Family-level inference only: AMELY is the Y-linked copy of amelogenin, so the dental and possible bone/marrow expression reported for AMELX may apply in males. No AMELY-specific non-dental evidence was found in this session.

The finding is a family-level inference with no AMELY-specific evidence, and the only tissue proposed (enamel organ, ameloblasts) is developmental. Nothing in the source supports AMELY expression in normal adult human non-reproductive tissue.
